# Text in ratatui::prelude - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/prelude/struct.Text.html

```
pub struct Text<'a> {
    pub alignment:
```
[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[HorizontalAlignment](https://docs.rs/enum.HorizontalAlignment.html)>,
    pub style: [Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html),
    pub lines: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Line](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html)<'a>>,
}## Expand description

A string split over one or more lines.

[ Text](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html) is used wherever text is displayed in the terminal and represents one or more

[s of text. When a](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html)

`Line`[is rendered, each line is rendered as a single line of text from top to bottom of the area. The text can be styled and aligned.](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html)

`Text`[§](https://docs.rs#constructor-methods)Constructor Methods

- `Text::raw`- `Text`(potentially multiple lines) with no style.
- `Text::styled`- `Text`(potentially multiple lines) with a style.
- `Text::default`- `Text`with empty content and the default style.

[§](https://docs.rs#conversion-methods)Conversion Methods

- `Text::from`- `Text`from a- `String`.
- `Text::from`- `Text`from a- `&str`.
- `Text::from`- `Text`from a- `Cow<str>`.
- `Text::from`- `Text`from a- `Span`
- `Text::from`- `Text`from a- `Line`
- `Text::from`- `Text`from a- `Vec<Line>`.
- `Text::from`- `Text`from a- `&[Into<Line>]`.
- `Text::from_iter`- `Text`from an iterator of items that can be converted into- `Line`.

[§](https://docs.rs#setter-methods)Setter Methods

These methods are fluent setters. They return a `Text` with the property set.

- `Text::style`- `Text`.
- `Text::alignment`- `Text`.
- `Text::left_aligned`- `Alignment::Left`
- `Text::centered`- `Alignment::Center`
- `Text::right_aligned`- `Alignment::Right`

[§](https://docs.rs#iteration-methods)Iteration Methods

- `Text::iter`
- `Text::iter_mut`
- `Text::into_iter`

[§](https://docs.rs#other-methods)Other Methods

- `Text::width`
- `Text::height`
- `Text::patch_style`- `Text`, adding modifiers from the given style.
- `Text::reset_style`- `Text`.
- `Text::push_line`
- `Text::push_span`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-text)Creating Text

A [ Text](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html), like a

[, can be constructed using one of the many](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html)

`Line``From` implementations or
via the [and](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html#method.raw)

`Text::raw`[methods. Helpfully,](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html#method.styled)

`Text::styled`[also implements](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html)

`Text`[which enables the concatenation of several](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.Extend.html)

`core::iter::Extend`[blocks.](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html)

`Text````
use std::borrow::Cow;
use std::iter;
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style, Stylize};
use ratatui_core::text::{Line, Span, Text};
let style = Style::new().yellow().italic();
let text = Text::raw("The first line\nThe second line").style(style);
let text = Text::styled("The first line\nThe second line", style);
let text = Text::styled(
    "The first line\nThe second line",
    (Color::Yellow, Modifier::ITALIC),
);
let text = Text::from("The first line\nThe second line");
let text = Text::from(String::from("The first line\nThe second line"));
let text = Text::from(Cow::Borrowed("The first line\nThe second line"));
let text = Text::from(Span::styled("The first line\nThe second line", style));
let text = Text::from(Line::from("The first line"));
let text = Text::from(vec![
    Line::from("The first line"),
    Line::from("The second line"),
]);
let text = Text::from_iter(iter::once("The first line").chain(iter::once("The second line")));
let mut text = Text::default();
text.extend(vec![
    Line::from("The first line"),
    Line::from("The second line"),
]);
text.extend(Text::from("The third line\nThe fourth line"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#styling-text)Styling Text

The text’s [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html) is used by the rendering widget to determine how to style the text. Each

[in the text will be styled with the](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html)

`Line`[of the text, and then with its own](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style``Text` also implements [which means you can use the methods of the](https://docs.rs/style/trait.Styled.html)

`Styled`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Stylize.html)

`Stylize````
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style, Stylize};
use ratatui_core::text::{Line, Text};
let text = Text::from("The first line\nThe second line").style(Style::new().yellow().italic());
let text = Text::from("The first line\nThe second line")
    .yellow()
    .italic();
let text = Text::from(vec![
    Line::from("The first line").yellow(),
    Line::from("The second line").yellow(),
])
.italic();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#aligning-text)Aligning Text

The text’s [ Alignment](https://docs.rs/type.Alignment.html) can be set using

[or the related helper methods. Lines composing the text can also be individually aligned with](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html#method.alignment)

`Text::alignment`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html#method.alignment)

`Line::alignment````
use ratatui_core::layout::Alignment;
use ratatui_core::text::{Line, Text};
let text = Text::from("The first line\nThe second line").alignment(Alignment::Right);
let text = Text::from("The first line\nThe second line").right_aligned();
let text = Text::from(vec![
    Line::from("The first line").left_aligned(),
    Line::from("The second line").right_aligned(),
    Line::from("The third line"),
])
.centered();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rendering-text)Rendering Text

`Text` implements the [ Widget](https://docs.rs/trait.Widget.html) trait, which means it can be rendered to a

[or to a](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)

`Buffer``Frame`.```
use ratatui_core::text::Text;
use ratatui_core::widgets::Widget;
// within another widget's `render` method:
let text = Text::from("The first line\nThe second line");
text.render(area, buf);
```
Or you can use the `render_widget` method on a `Frame` within a `Terminal::draw` closure.

[§](https://docs.rs#rendering-text-with-a-paragraph-widget)Rendering Text with a Paragraph Widget

Usually apps will use the `Paragraph` widget instead of rendering a `Text` directly as it
provides more functionality.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use ratatui::{
    buffer::Buffer,
    layout::Rect,
    text::Text,
    widgets::{Paragraph, Widget, Wrap},
};
let text = Text::from("The first line\nThe second line");
let paragraph = Paragraph::new(text)
    .wrap(Wrap { trim: true })
    .scroll((1, 1))
    .render(area, buf);
```

Sets the style of this text.

Defaults to [ Style::default()](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.default).

Note: This field was added in v0.26.0. Prior to that, the style of a text was determined
only by the style of each [ Line](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html) contained in the line. For this reason, this field may
not be supported by all widgets (outside of the

[Source](https://docs.rs/ratatui-core/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/ratatui_core/text/text.rs.html#367)

#### pub fn [patch_style](https://docs.rs#method.patch_style)<S>(self, style: S) -> [Text](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html)<'a>

Patches the style of this Text, adding modifiers from the given style.

This is useful for when you want to apply a style to a text that already has some styling.
In contrast to [ Text::style](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html#method.style), this method will not overwrite the existing style, but
instead will add the given style’s modifiers to this text’s style.

`Text` also implements [ Styled](https://docs.rs/style/trait.Styled.html) which means you can use the methods of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Stylize.html)

`Stylize``style` accepts any type that is convertible to [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html) (e.g.

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style`[, or your own type that implements](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)

`Color`[).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)

`Into<Style>`This is a fluent setter method which must be chained or used as it consumes self

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier};
use ratatui_core::text::Text;
let raw_text = Text::styled("The first line\nThe second line", Modifier::ITALIC);
let styled_text = Text::styled(
    String::from("The first line\nThe second line"),
    (Color::Yellow, Modifier::ITALIC),
);
assert_ne!(raw_text, styled_text);
let raw_text = raw_text.patch_style(Color::Yellow);
assert_eq!(raw_text, styled_text);
```

#### pub fn [reset_style](https://docs.rs#method.reset_style)(self) -> [Text](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html)<'a>

Resets the style of the Text.

Equivalent to calling [ patch_style(Style::reset())](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html#method.patch_style).

This is a fluent setter method which must be chained or used as it consumes self

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style};
use ratatui_core::text::Text;
let text = Text::styled(
    "The first line\nThe second line",
    (Color::Yellow, Modifier::ITALIC),
);
let text = text.reset_style();
assert_eq!(Style::reset(), text.style);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/ratatui-core/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/ratatui_core/text/text.rs.html#445)#### pub fn [alignment](https://docs.rs#method.alignment)(self, alignment: [HorizontalAlignment](https://docs.rs/enum.HorizontalAlignment.html)) -> [Text](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html)<'a>

[Source](https://docs.rs/ratatui-core/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/ratatui_core/text/text.rs.html#445)

#### pub fn [alignment](https://docs.rs#method.alignment)(self, alignment: [HorizontalAlignment](https://docs.rs/enum.HorizontalAlignment.html)) -> [Text](https://docs.rs/struct.Text.html)<'a>

Sets the alignment for this text.

Defaults to: [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None), meaning the alignment is determined by the rendering widget.
Setting the alignment of a Text generally overrides the alignment of its
parent Widget.

Alignment can be set individually on each line to override this text’s alignment.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

Set alignment to the whole text.

```
use ratatui_core::layout::Alignment;
use ratatui_core::text::Text;
let mut text = Text::from("Hi, what's up?");
assert_eq!(None, text.alignment);
assert_eq!(
    Some(Alignment::Right),
    text.alignment(Alignment::Right).alignment
)
```
Set a default alignment and override it on a per line basis.

```
use ratatui_core::layout::Alignment;
use ratatui_core::text::{Line, Text};
let text = Text::from(vec![
    Line::from("left").alignment(Alignment::Left),
    Line::from("default"),
    Line::from("default"),
    Line::from("right").alignment(Alignment::Right),
])
.alignment(Alignment::Center);
```
Will render the following

```
left
  default
  default
      right
```

Adds a line to the text.

`line` can be any type that can be converted into a `Line`. For example, you can pass a
`&str`, a `String`, a `Span`, or a `Line`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use ratatui_core::text::{Line, Span, Text};
let mut text = Text::from("Hello, world!");
text.push_line(Line::from("How are you?"));
text.push_line(Span::from("How are you?"));
text.push_line("How are you?");
```
Adds a span to the last line of the text.

`span` can be any type that is convertible into a `Span`. For example, you can pass a
`&str`, a `String`, or a `Span`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use ratatui_core::text::{Span, Text};
let mut text = Text::from("Hello, world!");
text.push_span(Span::from("How are you?"));
text.push_span("How are you?");

# Line in ratatui::prelude - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/prelude/struct.Line.html

```
pub struct Line<'a> {
    pub style:
```
[Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html),
    pub alignment: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[HorizontalAlignment](https://docs.rs/enum.HorizontalAlignment.html)>,
    pub spans: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)<'a>>,
}## Expand description

A line of text, consisting of one or more [ Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)s.

[ Line](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html)s are used wherever text is displayed in the terminal and represent a single line of
text. When a

[is rendered, it is rendered as a single line of text, with each](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html)

`Line`[being rendered in order (left to right).](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

`Span`Any newlines in the content are removed when creating a [ Line](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html) using the constructor or
conversion methods.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructor-methods)Constructor Methods

- `Line::default`
- `Line::raw`
- `Line::styled`

[§](https://docs.rs#conversion-methods)Conversion Methods

- `Line::from`- `Line`from a- `String`
- `Line::from`- `Line`from a- `&str`
- `Line::from`- `Line`from a- `Vec`- `Span`
- `Line::from`- `Line`from a- `&[Into<Span>]`.
- `Line::from`- `Line`from single- `Span`
- `String::from`- `String`
- `Line::from_iter`- `Span`

[§](https://docs.rs#setter-methods)Setter Methods

These methods are fluent setters. They return a `Line` with the property set.

- `Line::spans`
- `Line::style`
- `Line::alignment`
- `Line::left_aligned`- `Alignment::Left`
- `Line::centered`- `Alignment::Center`
- `Line::right_aligned`- `Alignment::Right`

[§](https://docs.rs#iteration-methods)Iteration Methods

- `Line::iter`
- `Line::iter_mut`
- `Line::into_iter`

[§](https://docs.rs#other-methods)Other Methods

- `Line::patch_style`
- `Line::reset_style`
- `Line::width`
- `Line::styled_graphemes`
- `Line::push_span`

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility-notes)Compatibility Notes

Before v0.26.0, [ Line](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html) did not have a

`style` field and instead relied on only the styles that
were set on each [contained in the](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

`Span``spans` field. The [method was the only way to set the overall style for individual lines. For this reason, this field may not be supported yet by all widgets (outside of the](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html#method.patch_style)

`Line::patch_style``ratatui` crate itself).[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-lines)Creating Lines

[ Line](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html)s can be created from

[s,](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

`Span`[s, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String`[s. They can be styled with a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

`&str`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style````
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style, Stylize};
use ratatui_core::text::{Line, Span};
let style = Style::new().yellow();
let line = Line::raw("Hello, world!").style(style);
let line = Line::styled("Hello, world!", style);
let line = Line::styled("Hello, world!", (Color::Yellow, Modifier::BOLD));
let line = Line::from("Hello, world!");
let line = Line::from(String::from("Hello, world!"));
let line = Line::from(vec![
    Span::styled("Hello", Style::new().blue()),
    Span::raw(" world!"),
]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#styling-lines)Styling Lines

The line’s [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html) is used by the rendering widget to determine how to style the line. Each

[in the line will be styled with the](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

`Span`[of the line, and then with its own](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style`[. If the line is longer than the available space, the style is applied to the entire line, and the line is truncated.](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style``Line` also implements [which means you can use the methods of the](https://docs.rs/style/trait.Styled.html)

`Styled`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Stylize.html)

`Stylize````
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style, Stylize};
use ratatui_core::text::Line;
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").style(Style::new().yellow().italic());
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").style(Color::Yellow);
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").style((Color::Yellow, Color::Black));
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").style((Color::Yellow, Modifier::ITALIC));
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").yellow().italic();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#aligning-lines)Aligning Lines

The line’s [ Alignment](https://docs.rs/type.Alignment.html) is used by the rendering widget to determine how to align the line
within the available space. If the line is longer than the available space, the alignment is
ignored and the line is truncated.

```
use ratatui_core::layout::Alignment;
use ratatui_core::text::Line;
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").alignment(Alignment::Right);
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").centered();
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").left_aligned();
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").right_aligned();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rendering-lines)Rendering Lines

`Line` implements the [ Widget](https://docs.rs/trait.Widget.html) trait, which means it can be rendered to a

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)

`Buffer````
use ratatui_core::buffer::Buffer;
use ratatui_core::layout::Rect;
use ratatui_core::style::{Style, Stylize};
use ratatui_core::text::Line;
use ratatui_core::widgets::Widget;
// in another widget's render method
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").style(Style::new().yellow().italic());
line.render(area, buf);
```
Or you can use the `render_widget` method on the `Frame` in a `Terminal::draw` closure.

[§](https://docs.rs#rendering-lines-with-a-paragraph-widget)Rendering Lines with a Paragraph widget

Usually apps will use the `Paragraph` widget instead of rendering a [ Line](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html) directly as it
provides more functionality.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use ratatui::{
    buffer::Buffer,
    layout::Rect,
    style::Stylize,
    text::Line,
    widgets::{Paragraph, Widget, Wrap},
};
let line = Line::from("Hello world!").yellow().italic();
Paragraph::new(line)
    .wrap(Wrap { trim: true })
    .render(area, buf);
```

        .collect::<Vec<StyledGrapheme>>(),

        StyledGrapheme::new("e", Style::default().fg(Color::Yellow).bg(Color::Black)),

[Source](https://docs.rs/ratatui-core/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/ratatui_core/text/line.rs.html#512)#### pub fn [patch_style](https://docs.rs#method.patch_style)<S>(self, style: S) -> [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html)<'a>

[Source](https://docs.rs/ratatui-core/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/ratatui_core/text/line.rs.html#512)

#### pub fn [patch_style](https://docs.rs#method.patch_style)<S>(self, style: S) -> [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html)<'a>

Patches the style of this Line, adding modifiers from the given style.

This is useful for when you want to apply a style to a line that already has some styling.
In contrast to [ Line::style](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html#method.style), this method will not overwrite the existing style, but
instead will add the given style’s modifiers to this Line’s style.

`style` accepts any type that is convertible to [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html) (e.g.

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style`[, or your own type that implements](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)

`Color`[).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)

`Into<Style>`This is a fluent setter method which must be chained or used as it consumes self

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier};
use ratatui_core::text::Line;
let line = Line::styled("My text", Modifier::ITALIC);
let styled_line = Line::styled("My text", (Color::Yellow, Modifier::ITALIC));
assert_eq!(styled_line, line.patch_style(Color::Yellow));
```

# Span in ratatui::prelude - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/prelude/struct.Span.html

## Expand description

Represents a part of a line that is contiguous and where all characters share the same style.

A `Span` is the smallest unit of text that can be styled. It is usually combined in the [ Line](https://docs.rs/struct.Line.html)
type to represent a line of text where each

`Span` may have a different style.[§](https://docs.rs#constructor-methods)Constructor Methods

- `Span::default`
- `Span::raw`
- `Span::styled`

[§](https://docs.rs#setter-methods)Setter Methods

These methods are fluent setters. They return a new `Span` with the specified property set.

- `Span::content`
- `Span::style`

[§](https://docs.rs#other-methods)Other Methods

- `Span::patch_style`
- `Span::reset_style`
- `Span::width`
- `Span::styled_graphemes`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

A `Span` with `style` set to [ Style::default()](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.default) can be created from a

`&str`, a `String`, or
any type convertible to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/enum.Cow.html)

`Cow<str>````
use ratatui_core::text::Span;
let span = Span::raw("test content");
let span = Span::raw(String::from("test content"));
let span = Span::from("test content");
let span = Span::from(String::from("test content"));
let span: Span = "test content".into();
let span: Span = String::from("test content").into();
```
Styled spans can be created using [ Span::styled](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.styled) or by converting strings using methods from
the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Stylize.html)

`Stylize````
use ratatui_core::style::{Style, Stylize};
use ratatui_core::text::Span;
let span = Span::styled("test content", Style::new().green());
let span = Span::styled(String::from("test content"), Style::new().green());
// using Stylize trait shortcuts
let span = "test content".green();
let span = String::from("test content").green();
```
`Span` implements the [ Styled](https://docs.rs/style/trait.Styled.html) trait, which allows it to be styled using the shortcut methods
defined in the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Stylize.html)

`Stylize````
use ratatui_core::style::Stylize;
use ratatui_core::text::Span;
let span = Span::raw("test content").green().on_yellow().italic();
let span = Span::raw(String::from("test content"))
    .green()
    .on_yellow()
    .italic();
```
`Span` implements the [ Widget](https://docs.rs/trait.Widget.html) trait, which allows it to be rendered to a

[. Often apps will use the](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)

`Buffer``Paragraph` widget instead of rendering `Span` directly, as it handles text
wrapping and alignment for you.## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.style)

`style: `[Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)The style of the span.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.content)

`content: `[Cow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/enum.Cow.html)<'a, [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>The content of the span as a Clone-on-write string.

# ratatui::style - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/style/index.html

## Expand description

`style` contains the primitives used to control how your user interface will look.

There are two ways to set styles:

- Creating and using the `Style``Style::new().fg(Color::Red)`).
- Using style shorthands. (e.g. `"hello".red()`).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-style-struct)Using the `Style` struct

This is the original approach to styling and likely the most common. This is useful when creating style variables to reuse, however the shorthands are often more convenient and readable for most use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style};
use ratatui_core::text::Span;
let heading_style = Style::new()
    .fg(Color::Black)
    .bg(Color::Green)
    .add_modifier(Modifier::ITALIC | Modifier::BOLD);
let span = Span::styled("hello", heading_style);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-style-shorthands)Using style shorthands

Originally Ratatui only had the ability to set styles using the `Style` struct. This is still
supported, but there are now shorthands for all the styles that can be set. These save you from
having to create a `Style` struct every time you want to set a style.

The shorthands are implemented in the [ Stylize](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Stylize.html) trait which is automatically implemented for
many types via the

[trait. This means that you can use the shorthands on any type that implements](https://docs.rs/trait.Styled.html)

`Styled`[. E.g.:](https://docs.rs/trait.Styled.html)

`Styled`- Strings and string slices when styled return a `Span`
- `Span`
- Many widget types can be styled directly rather than calling their `style()`method.

See the [ Stylize](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Stylize.html) and

[traits for more information.](https://docs.rs/trait.Styled.html)

`Styled`[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style, Stylize};
use ratatui_core::text::{Span, Text};
assert_eq!(
    "hello".red().on_blue().bold(),
    Span::styled(
        "hello",
        Style::default()
            .fg(Color::Red)
            .bg(Color::Blue)
            .add_modifier(Modifier::BOLD)
    )
);
assert_eq!(
    Text::from("hello").red().on_blue().bold(),
    Text::from("hello").style(
        Style::default()
            .fg(Color::Red)
            .bg(Color::Blue)
            .add_modifier(Modifier::BOLD)
    )
);
```

# Style in ratatui::prelude - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/prelude/struct.Style.html

```
pub struct Style {
    pub fg:
```
[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Color](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)>,
    pub bg: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Color](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)>,
    pub underline_color: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Color](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)>,
    pub add_modifier: [Modifier](https://docs.rs/struct.Modifier.html),
    pub sub_modifier: [Modifier](https://docs.rs/struct.Modifier.html),
}## Expand description

Style lets you control the main characteristics of the displayed elements.

```
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style};
Style::default()
    .fg(Color::Black)
    .bg(Color::Green)
    .add_modifier(Modifier::ITALIC | Modifier::BOLD);
```
Styles can also be created with a [shorthand notation](https://docs.rs/style/index.html#using-style-shorthands).

```
use ratatui_core::style::{Style, Stylize};
Style::new().black().on_green().italic().bold();
```
For more information about the style shorthands, see the [ Stylize](https://docs.rs/trait.Stylize.html) trait.

We implement conversions from [ Color](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html) and

[to](https://docs.rs/struct.Modifier.html)

`Modifier`[so you can use them anywhere that accepts](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style``Into<Style>`.```
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style};
use ratatui_core::text::Line;
Line::styled("hello", Style::new().fg(Color::Red));
// simplifies to
Line::styled("hello", Color::Red);
Line::styled("hello", Style::new().add_modifier(Modifier::BOLD));
// simplifies to
Line::styled("hello", Modifier::BOLD);
```
Styles represents an incremental change. If you apply the styles S1, S2, S3 to a cell of the terminal buffer, the style of this cell will be the result of the merge of S1, S2 and S3, not just S3.

```
use ratatui_core::buffer::Buffer;
use ratatui_core::layout::Rect;
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style};
let styles = [
    Style::default()
        .fg(Color::Blue)
        .add_modifier(Modifier::BOLD | Modifier::ITALIC),
    Style::default()
        .bg(Color::Red)
        .add_modifier(Modifier::UNDERLINED),
    #[cfg(feature = "underline-color")]
    Style::default().underline_color(Color::Green),
    Style::default()
        .fg(Color::Yellow)
        .remove_modifier(Modifier::ITALIC),
];
let mut buffer = Buffer::empty(Rect::new(0, 0, 1, 1));
for style in &styles {
    buffer[(0, 0)].set_style(*style);
}
assert_eq!(
    Style {
        fg: Some(Color::Yellow),
        bg: Some(Color::Red),
        #[cfg(feature = "underline-color")]
        underline_color: Some(Color::Green),
        add_modifier: Modifier::BOLD | Modifier::UNDERLINED,
        sub_modifier: Modifier::empty(),
    },
    buffer[(0, 0)].style(),
);
```
The default implementation returns a `Style` that does not modify anything. If you wish to
reset all properties until that point use [ Style::reset](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.reset).

```
use ratatui_core::buffer::Buffer;
use ratatui_core::layout::Rect;
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style};
let styles = [
    Style::default()
        .fg(Color::Blue)
        .add_modifier(Modifier::BOLD | Modifier::ITALIC),
    Style::reset().fg(Color::Yellow),
];
let mut buffer = Buffer::empty(Rect::new(0, 0, 1, 1));
for style in &styles {
    buffer[(0, 0)].set_style(*style);
}
assert_eq!(
    Style {
        fg: Some(Color::Yellow),
        bg: Some(Color::Reset),
        #[cfg(feature = "underline-color")]
        underline_color: Some(Color::Reset),
        add_modifier: Modifier::empty(),
        sub_modifier: Modifier::empty(),
    },
    buffer[(0, 0)].style(),
);
```

**crate feature**only.

`underline-color`Changes the underline color. The text must be underlined with a modifier for this to work.

This uses a non-standard ANSI escape sequence. It is supported by most terminal emulators,
but is only implemented in the crossterm backend and enabled by the `underline-color`
feature flag.

See
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#SGR_(Select_Graphic_Rendition)_parameters)
code `58` and `59` for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use ratatui_core::style::{Color, Modifier, Style};
let style = Style::default()
    .underline_color(Color::Blue)
    .add_modifier(Modifier::UNDERLINED);
let diff = Style::default()
    .underline_color(Color::Red)
    .add_modifier(Modifier::UNDERLINED);
assert_eq!(
    style.patch(diff),
    Style::default()
        .underline_color(Color::Red)
        .add_modifier(Modifier::UNDERLINED)
);
```

}## Expand description

An extension trait for styling objects.

For any type that implements `Stylize`, the provided methods in this trait can be used to style
the type further. This trait is automatically implemented for any type that implements the
[ Styled](https://docs.rs/style/trait.Styled.html) trait which e.g.:

[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

`&str`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

`Span`[and many Widget types.](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style`This results in much more ergonomic styling of text and widgets. For example, instead of writing:

You can write:

This trait implements a provided method for every color as both foreground and background
(prefixed by `on_`), and all modifiers as both an additive and subtractive modifier (prefixed
by `not_`). The `reset()` method is also provided to reset the style.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use ratatui_core::{
    style::{Color, Modifier, Style, Stylize},
    text::Line,
    widgets::{Block, Paragraph},
};
let span = "hello".red().on_blue().bold();
let line = Line::from(vec![
    "hello".red().on_blue().bold(),
    "world".green().on_yellow().not_bold(),
]);
let paragraph = Paragraph::new(line).italic().underlined();
let block = Block::bordered().title("Title").on_white().bold();
```

# CrosstermBackend in ratatui::backend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/backend/struct.CrosstermBackend.html

`pub struct CrosstermBackend<W>{ /* private fields */ }`**crate feature**only.

`crossterm`## Expand description

A [ Backend](https://docs.rs/prelude/backend/index.html) implementation that uses

[Crossterm](https://crates.io/crates/crossterm)to render to the terminal.

The `CrosstermBackend` struct is a wrapper around a writer implementing [ Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html), which is
used to send commands to the terminal. It provides methods for drawing content, manipulating
the cursor, and clearing the terminal screen.

Most applications should not call the methods on `CrosstermBackend` directly, but will instead
use the [ Terminal](https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/struct.Terminal.html) struct, which provides a more ergonomic interface.

Usually applications will enable raw mode and switch to alternate screen mode after creating
a `CrosstermBackend`. This is done by calling [ crossterm::terminal::enable_raw_mode](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/terminal/fn.enable_raw_mode.html) and

[(and the corresponding disable/leave functions when the application exits). This is not done automatically by the backend because it is possible that the application may want to use the terminal for other purposes (like showing help text) before entering alternate screen mode.](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/terminal/struct.EnterAlternateScreen.html)

`crossterm::terminal::EnterAlternateScreen`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::io::{stderr, stdout};
use crossterm::ExecutableCommand;
use crossterm::terminal::{
    EnterAlternateScreen, LeaveAlternateScreen, disable_raw_mode, enable_raw_mode,
};
use ratatui::Terminal;
use ratatui::backend::CrosstermBackend;
let mut backend = CrosstermBackend::new(stdout());
// or
let backend = CrosstermBackend::new(stderr());
let mut terminal = Terminal::new(backend)?;
enable_raw_mode()?;
stdout().execute(EnterAlternateScreen)?;
terminal.clear()?;
terminal.draw(|frame| {
    // -- snip --
})?;
stdout().execute(LeaveAlternateScreen)?;
disable_raw_mode()?;
```
See the [Examples](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/tree/main/ratatui/examples/README.md) directory for more examples. See the [ backend](https://docs.rs/prelude/backend/index.html) module documentation
for more details on raw mode and alternate screen.

### impl<T> [ExecutableCommand](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.ExecutableCommand.html) for T

Executes the given command directly.

The given command its ANSI escape code will be written and flushed onto `Self`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

-
The command that you want to execute directly.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use std::io;
use crossterm::{ExecutableCommand, style::Print};
fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
     // will be executed directly
      io::stdout()
        .execute(Print("sum:\n".to_string()))?
        .execute(Print(format!("1 + 1= {} ", 1 + 1)))?;
      Ok(())
     // ==== Output ====
     // sum:
     // 1 + 1 = 2
}
```
Have a look over at the [Command API](https://docs.rs/index.html#command-api) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

- In the case of UNIX and Windows 10, ANSI codes are written to the given ‘writer’.
- In case of Windows versions lower than 10, a direct WinAPI call will be made.
The reason for this is that Windows versions lower than 10 do not support ANSI codes,
and can therefore not be written to the given `writer`. Therefore, there is no difference between[execute](https://docs.rs/trait.ExecutableCommand.html)and[queue](https://docs.rs/trait.QueueableCommand.html)for those old Windows versions.

### impl<T> [QueueableCommand](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.QueueableCommand.html) for T

Queues the given command for further execution.

Queued commands will be executed in the following cases:

- When `flush`is called manually on the given type implementing`io::Write`.
- The terminal will `flush`automatically if the buffer is full.
- Each line is flushed in case of `stdout`, because it is line buffered.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments-1)Arguments

-
The command that you want to queue for later execution.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::io::{self, Write};
use crossterm::{QueueableCommand, style::Print};
 fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut stdout = io::stdout();
    // `Print` will executed executed when `flush` is called.
    stdout
        .queue(Print("foo 1\n".to_string()))?
        .queue(Print("foo 2".to_string()))?;
    // some other code (no execution happening here) ...
    // when calling `flush` on `stdout`, all commands will be written to the stdout and therefore executed.
    stdout.flush()?;
    Ok(())
    // ==== Output ====
    // foo 1
    // foo 2
}
```
Have a look over at the [Command API](https://docs.rs/index.html#command-api) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes-1)Notes

- In the case of UNIX and Windows 10, ANSI codes are written to the given ‘writer’.
- In case of Windows versions lower than 10, a direct WinAPI call will be made.
The reason for this is that Windows versions lower than 10 do not support ANSI codes,
and can therefore not be written to the given `writer`. Therefore, there is no difference between[execute](https://docs.rs/trait.ExecutableCommand.html)and[queue](https://docs.rs/trait.QueueableCommand.html)for those old Windows versions.

[Source](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/crossterm/command.rs.html#191)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-SynchronizedUpdate-for-W)### impl<W> [SynchronizedUpdate](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.SynchronizedUpdate.html) for W

[Source](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/crossterm/command.rs.html#191)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-SynchronizedUpdate-for-W)

### impl<W> [SynchronizedUpdate](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.SynchronizedUpdate.html) for W

Performs a set of actions within a synchronous update.

Updates will be suspended in the terminal, the function will be executed against self, updates will be resumed, and a flush will be performed.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments-2)Arguments

-
Function A function that performs the operations that must execute in a synchronized update.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use std::io;
use crossterm::{ExecutableCommand, SynchronizedUpdate, style::Print};
fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut stdout = io::stdout();
    stdout.sync_update(|stdout| {
        stdout.execute(Print("foo 1\n".to_string()))?;
        stdout.execute(Print("foo 2".to_string()))?;
        // The effects of the print command will not be present in the terminal
        // buffer, but not visible in the terminal.
        std::io::Result::Ok(())
    })?;
    // The effects of the commands will be visible.
    Ok(())
    // ==== Output ====
    // foo 1
    // foo 2
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#notes-2)Notes

This command is performed only using ANSI codes, and will do nothing on terminals that do not support ANSI codes, or this specific extension.

When rendering the screen of the terminal, the Emulator usually iterates through each visible grid cell and renders its current state. With applications updating the screen a at higher frequency this can cause tearing.

This mode attempts to mitigate that.

When the synchronization mode is enabled following render calls will keep rendering the last rendered state. The terminal Emulator keeps processing incoming text and sequences. When the synchronized update mode is disabled again the renderer may fetch the latest screen buffer state again, effectively avoiding the tearing effect by unintentionally rendering in the middle a of an application screen update.

[Source](https://docs.rs/palette/0.7.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/palette/cast/from_into_components_traits.rs.html#584-586)

# crossterm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cross-platform-terminal-manipulation-library)Cross-platform Terminal Manipulation Library

Crossterm is a pure-rust, terminal manipulation library that makes it possible to write cross-platform text-based interfaces.

This crate supports all UNIX and Windows terminals down to Windows 7 (not all terminals are tested
see [Tested Terminals](https://github.com/crossterm-rs/crossterm#tested-terminals)
for more info).

[§](https://docs.rs#command-api)Command API

The command API makes the use of `crossterm` much easier and offers more control over when and how a
command is executed. A command is just an action you can perform on the terminal e.g. cursor movement.

The command API offers:

- Better Performance.
- Complete control over when to flush.
- Complete control over where the ANSI escape commands are executed to.
- Way easier and nicer API.

There are two ways to use the API command:

- Functions can execute commands on types that implement Write. Functions are easier to use and debug. There is a disadvantage, and that is that there is a boilerplate code involved.
- Macros are generally seen as more difficult and aren’t always well supported by editors but offer an API with less boilerplate code. If you are not afraid of macros, this is a recommendation.

Linux and Windows 10 systems support ANSI escape codes. Those ANSI escape codes are strings or rather a
byte sequence. When we `write` and `flush` those to the terminal we can perform some action.
For older windows systems a WinAPI call is made.

[§](https://docs.rs#command-execution)Command Execution

There are two different ways to execute commands:

[§](https://docs.rs#lazy-execution)Lazy Execution

Flushing bytes to the terminal buffer is a heavy system call. If we perform a lot of actions with the terminal, we want to do this periodically - like with a TUI editor - so that we can flush more data to the terminal buffer at the same time.

Crossterm offers the possibility to do this with `queue`.
With `queue` you can queue commands, and when you call [Write::flush](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html#tymethod.flush) these commands will be executed.

You can pass a custom buffer implementing [std::io::Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html) to this `queue` operation.
The commands will be executed on that buffer.
The most common buffer is [std::io::stdout](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/fn.stdout.html) however, [std::io::stderr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/fn.stderr.html) is used sometimes as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

A simple demonstration that shows the command API in action with cursor commands.

Functions:

```
use std::io::{Write, stdout};
use crossterm::{QueueableCommand, cursor};
let mut stdout = stdout();
stdout.queue(cursor::MoveTo(5,5));
// some other code ...
stdout.flush();
```
The [queue](https://docs.rs/trait.QueueableCommand.html) function returns itself, therefore you can use this to queue another
command. Like `stdout.queue(Goto(5,5)).queue(Clear(ClearType::All))`.

Macros:

```
use std::io::{Write, stdout};
use crossterm::{queue, QueueableCommand, cursor};
let mut stdout = stdout();
queue!(stdout,  cursor::MoveTo(5, 5));
// some other code ...
// move operation is performed only if we flush the buffer.
stdout.flush();
```
You can pass more than one command into the [queue](https://docs.rs/macro.queue.html) macro like
`queue!(stdout, MoveTo(5, 5), Clear(ClearType::All))` and
they will be executed in the given order from left to right.

[§](https://docs.rs#direct-execution)Direct Execution

For many applications it is not at all important to be efficient with ‘flush’ operations.
For this use case there is the `execute` operation.
This operation executes the command immediately, and calls the `flush` under water.

You can pass a custom buffer implementing [std::io::Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html) to this `execute` operation.
The commands will be executed on that buffer.
The most common buffer is [std::io::stdout](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/fn.stdout.html) however, [std::io::stderr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/fn.stderr.html) is used sometimes as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

Functions:

```
use std::io::{Write, stdout};
use crossterm::{ExecutableCommand, cursor};
let mut stdout = stdout();
stdout.execute(cursor::MoveTo(5,5));
```
The [execute](https://docs.rs/trait.ExecutableCommand.html) function returns itself, therefore you can use this to queue
another command. Like `stdout.execute(Goto(5,5))?.execute(Clear(ClearType::All))`.

Macros:

```
use std::io::{stdout, Write};
use crossterm::{execute, ExecutableCommand, cursor};
let mut stdout = stdout();
execute!(stdout, cursor::MoveTo(5, 5));
```
You can pass more than one command into the [execute](https://docs.rs/macro.execute.html) macro like
`execute!(stdout, MoveTo(5, 5), Clear(ClearType::All))` and they will be executed in the given order from
left to right.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

Print a rectangle colored with magenta and use both direct execution and lazy execution.

Functions:

```
use std::io::{self, Write};
use crossterm::{
    ExecutableCommand, QueueableCommand,
    terminal, cursor, style::{self, Stylize}
};
fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
  let mut stdout = io::stdout();
  stdout.execute(terminal::Clear(terminal::ClearType::All))?;
  for y in 0..40 {
    for x in 0..150 {
      if (y == 0 || y == 40 - 1) || (x == 0 || x == 150 - 1) {
        // in this loop we are more efficient by not flushing the buffer.
        stdout
          .queue(cursor::MoveTo(x,y))?
          .queue(style::PrintStyledContent( "█".magenta()))?;
      }
    }
  }
  stdout.flush()?;
  Ok(())
}
```
Macros:

```
use std::io::{self, Write};
use crossterm::{
    execute, queue,
    style::{self, Stylize}, cursor, terminal
};
fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
  let mut stdout = io::stdout();
  execute!(stdout, terminal::Clear(terminal::ClearType::All))?;
  for y in 0..40 {
    for x in 0..150 {
      if (y == 0 || y == 40 - 1) || (x == 0 || x == 150 - 1) {
        // in this loop we are more efficient by not flushing the buffer.
        queue!(stdout, cursor::MoveTo(x,y), style::PrintStyledContent( "█".magenta()))?;
      }
    }
  }
  stdout.flush()?;
  Ok(())
}
```

# TermionBackend in ratatui::backend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/backend/struct.TermionBackend.html

`pub struct TermionBackend<W>{ /* private fields */ }`**crate feature**only.

`termion` and non-Windows## Expand description

A [ Backend](https://docs.rs/trait.Backend.html) implementation that uses

[Termion](https://docs.rs/termion)to render to the terminal.

The `TermionBackend` struct is a wrapper around a writer implementing [ Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html), which is used
to send commands to the terminal. It provides methods for drawing content, manipulating the
cursor, and clearing the terminal screen.

Most applications should not call the methods on `TermionBackend` directly, but will instead
use the [ Terminal](https://docs.rs/struct.Terminal.html) struct, which provides a more ergonomic interface.

Usually applications will enable raw mode and switch to alternate screen mode when starting.
This is done by calling [ IntoRawMode::into_raw_mode()](https://docs.rs/termion/4.0.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/termion/raw/trait.IntoRawMode.html) and

[on the writer before creating the backend. This is not done automatically by the backend because it is possible that the application may want to use the terminal for other purposes (like showing help text) before entering alternate screen mode. This backend automatically disable raw mode and switches back to the primary screen when the writer is dropped.](https://docs.rs/termion/4.0.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/termion/screen/trait.IntoAlternateScreen.html)

`IntoAlternateScreen::into_alternate_screen()`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::io::{stderr, stdout};
use ratatui::Terminal;
use ratatui::backend::TermionBackend;
use ratatui::termion::raw::IntoRawMode;
use ratatui::termion::screen::IntoAlternateScreen;
let writer = stdout().into_raw_mode()?.into_alternate_screen()?;
let mut backend = TermionBackend::new(writer);
// or
let writer = stderr().into_raw_mode()?.into_alternate_screen()?;
let backend = TermionBackend::new(stderr());
let mut terminal = Terminal::new(backend)?;
terminal.clear()?;
terminal.draw(|frame| {
    // -- snip --
})?;
```

### impl<T> [ExecutableCommand](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.ExecutableCommand.html) for T

Executes the given command directly.

The given command its ANSI escape code will be written and flushed onto `Self`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

-
The command that you want to execute directly.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use std::io;
use crossterm::{ExecutableCommand, style::Print};
fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
     // will be executed directly
      io::stdout()
        .execute(Print("sum:\n".to_string()))?
        .execute(Print(format!("1 + 1= {} ", 1 + 1)))?;
      Ok(())
     // ==== Output ====
     // sum:
     // 1 + 1 = 2
}
```
Have a look over at the [Command API](https://docs.rs/index.html#command-api) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

- In the case of UNIX and Windows 10, ANSI codes are written to the given ‘writer’.
- In case of Windows versions lower than 10, a direct WinAPI call will be made.
The reason for this is that Windows versions lower than 10 do not support ANSI codes,
and can therefore not be written to the given `writer`. Therefore, there is no difference between[execute](https://docs.rs/trait.ExecutableCommand.html)and[queue](https://docs.rs/trait.QueueableCommand.html)for those old Windows versions.

### impl<T> [QueueableCommand](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.QueueableCommand.html) for T

Queues the given command for further execution.

Queued commands will be executed in the following cases:

- When `flush`is called manually on the given type implementing`io::Write`.
- The terminal will `flush`automatically if the buffer is full.
- Each line is flushed in case of `stdout`, because it is line buffered.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments-1)Arguments

-
The command that you want to queue for later execution.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::io::{self, Write};
use crossterm::{QueueableCommand, style::Print};
 fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut stdout = io::stdout();
    // `Print` will executed executed when `flush` is called.
    stdout
        .queue(Print("foo 1\n".to_string()))?
        .queue(Print("foo 2".to_string()))?;
    // some other code (no execution happening here) ...
    // when calling `flush` on `stdout`, all commands will be written to the stdout and therefore executed.
    stdout.flush()?;
    Ok(())
    // ==== Output ====
    // foo 1
    // foo 2
}
```
Have a look over at the [Command API](https://docs.rs/index.html#command-api) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes-1)Notes

- In the case of UNIX and Windows 10, ANSI codes are written to the given ‘writer’.
- In case of Windows versions lower than 10, a direct WinAPI call will be made.
The reason for this is that Windows versions lower than 10 do not support ANSI codes,
and can therefore not be written to the given `writer`. Therefore, there is no difference between[execute](https://docs.rs/trait.ExecutableCommand.html)and[queue](https://docs.rs/trait.QueueableCommand.html)for those old Windows versions.

[Source](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/crossterm/command.rs.html#191)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-SynchronizedUpdate-for-W)### impl<W> [SynchronizedUpdate](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.SynchronizedUpdate.html) for W

[Source](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/crossterm/command.rs.html#191)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-SynchronizedUpdate-for-W)

### impl<W> [SynchronizedUpdate](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.SynchronizedUpdate.html) for W

Performs a set of actions within a synchronous update.

Updates will be suspended in the terminal, the function will be executed against self, updates will be resumed, and a flush will be performed.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments-2)Arguments

-
Function A function that performs the operations that must execute in a synchronized update.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use std::io;
use crossterm::{ExecutableCommand, SynchronizedUpdate, style::Print};
fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut stdout = io::stdout();
    stdout.sync_update(|stdout| {
        stdout.execute(Print("foo 1\n".to_string()))?;
        stdout.execute(Print("foo 2".to_string()))?;
        // The effects of the print command will not be present in the terminal
        // buffer, but not visible in the terminal.
        std::io::Result::Ok(())
    })?;
    // The effects of the commands will be visible.
    Ok(())
    // ==== Output ====
    // foo 1
    // foo 2
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#notes-2)Notes

This command is performed only using ANSI codes, and will do nothing on terminals that do not support ANSI codes, or this specific extension.

When rendering the screen of the terminal, the Emulator usually iterates through each visible grid cell and renders its current state. With applications updating the screen a at higher frequency this can cause tearing.

This mode attempts to mitigate that.

When the synchronization mode is enabled following render calls will keep rendering the last rendered state. The terminal Emulator keeps processing incoming text and sequences. When the synchronized update mode is disabled again the renderer may fetch the latest screen buffer state again, effectively avoiding the tearing effect by unintentionally rendering in the middle a of an application screen update.

[Source](https://docs.rs/palette/0.7.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/palette/cast/from_into_components_traits.rs.html#584-586)

# termion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/termion/4.0.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/termion/index.html

## Expand description

Termion is a pure Rust, bindless library for low-level handling, manipulating and reading information about terminals. This provides a full-featured alternative to Termbox.

Termion aims to be simple and yet expressive. It is bindless, meaning that it is not a front-end to some other library (e.g., ncurses or termbox), but a standalone library directly talking to the TTY.

Supports Redox, Mac OS X, and Linux (or, in general, ANSI terminals).

For more information refer to the [README](https://github.com/redox-os/termion).

`termina`## Expand description

A [ Backend](https://docs.rs/trait.Backend.html) implementation that renders through a

[.](https://docs.rs/termina/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/termina/terminal/trait.Terminal.html)

`termina::Terminal``TerminaBackend` writes typed Termina escape sequences for drawing, cursor control, clearing,
and terminal-size queries.

This backend does not automatically enable raw mode or switch to the alternate screen. Use Termina’s terminal APIs and typed escape sequences to configure those application-level modes before drawing.

})?;
```

### impl<T> [QueueableCommand](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.QueueableCommand.html) for T

Queues the given command for further execution.

Queued commands will be executed in the following cases:

- When `flush`is called manually on the given type implementing`io::Write`.
- The terminal will `flush`automatically if the buffer is full.
- Each line is flushed in case of `stdout`, because it is line buffered.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments-1)Arguments

-
The command that you want to queue for later execution.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::io::{self, Write};
use crossterm::{QueueableCommand, style::Print};
 fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut stdout = io::stdout();
    // `Print` will executed executed when `flush` is called.
    stdout
        .queue(Print("foo 1\n".to_string()))?
        .queue(Print("foo 2".to_string()))?;
    // some other code (no execution happening here) ...
    // when calling `flush` on `stdout`, all commands will be written to the stdout and therefore executed.
    stdout.flush()?;
    Ok(())
    // ==== Output ====
    // foo 1
    // foo 2
}
```
Have a look over at the [Command API](https://docs.rs/index.html#command-api) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes-1)Notes

- In the case of UNIX and Windows 10, ANSI codes are written to the given ‘writer’.
- In case of Windows versions lower than 10, a direct WinAPI call will be made.
The reason for this is that Windows versions lower than 10 do not support ANSI codes,
and can therefore not be written to the given `writer`. Therefore, there is no difference between[execute](https://docs.rs/trait.ExecutableCommand.html)and[queue](https://docs.rs/trait.QueueableCommand.html)for those old Windows versions.

[Source](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/crossterm/command.rs.html#191)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-SynchronizedUpdate-for-W)### impl<W> [SynchronizedUpdate](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.SynchronizedUpdate.html) for W

[Source](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/crossterm/command.rs.html#191)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-SynchronizedUpdate-for-W)

### impl<W> [SynchronizedUpdate](https://docs.rs/crossterm/0.29.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossterm/command/trait.SynchronizedUpdate.html) for W

Performs a set of actions within a synchronous update.

Updates will be suspended in the terminal, the function will be executed against self, updates will be resumed, and a flush will be performed.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments-2)Arguments

-
Function A function that performs the operations that must execute in a synchronized update.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use std::io;
use crossterm::{ExecutableCommand, SynchronizedUpdate, style::Print};
fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut stdout = io::stdout();
    stdout.sync_update(|stdout| {
        stdout.execute(Print("foo 1\n".to_string()))?;
        stdout.execute(Print("foo 2".to_string()))?;
        // The effects of the print command will not be present in the terminal
        // buffer, but not visible in the terminal.
        std::io::Result::Ok(())
    })?;
    // The effects of the commands will be visible.
    Ok(())
    // ==== Output ====
    // foo 1
    // foo 2
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#notes-2)Notes

This command is performed only using ANSI codes, and will do nothing on terminals that do not support ANSI codes, or this specific extension.

When rendering the screen of the terminal, the Emulator usually iterates through each visible grid cell and renders its current state. With applications updating the screen a at higher frequency this can cause tearing.

This mode attempts to mitigate that.

When the synchronization mode is enabled following render calls will keep rendering the last rendered state. The terminal Emulator keeps processing incoming text and sequences. When the synchronized update mode is disabled again the renderer may fetch the latest screen buffer state again, effectively avoiding the tearing effect by unintentionally rendering in the middle a of an application screen update.

[Source](https://docs.rs/palette/0.7.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/palette/cast/from_into_components_traits.rs.html#584-586)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-TryComponentsInto%3CC%3E-for-T)### impl<T, C> [TryComponentsInto](https://docs.rs/palette/0.7.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/palette/cast/from_into_components_traits/trait.TryComponentsInto.html)<C> for T

[Source](https://docs.rs/palette/0.7.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/palette/cast/from_into_components_traits.rs.html#584-586)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-TryComponentsInto%3CC%3E-for-T)

# termina - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/termina/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/termina/index.html

## Expand description

Terminal I/O, escape-sequence types, styling, and input parsing.

Termina keeps the terminal protocol visible. Applications write typed CSI, OSC, and DCS values
from [ escape](https://docs.rs/escape/index.html) instead of assembling byte strings, and read typed

[values instead of decoding terminal input by hand.](https://docs.rs/event/enum.Event.html)

`Event`[opens the current process terminal, switches raw/cooked mode, writes bytes, and creates an](https://docs.rs/type.PlatformTerminal.html)

`PlatformTerminal`[for synchronous input.](https://docs.rs/struct.EventReader.html)

`EventReader`Code that already has terminal bytes can use [ Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html) directly. That is useful for PTY tests,
terminal multiplexers, or callers that own the input source and only need Termina’s parser.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::io::{self, Write};
use termina::{
    event::{KeyCode, KeyEventKind},
    Event, PlatformTerminal, Terminal,
};
fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut terminal = PlatformTerminal::new()?;
    terminal.enter_raw_mode()?;
    writeln!(terminal, "Press q to exit.")?;
    let reader = terminal.event_reader();
    loop {
        let event = reader.read(|_| true)?;
        if matches!(
            event,
            Event::Key(key)
                if key.kind == KeyEventKind::Press && key.code == KeyCode::Char('q')
        ) {
            break;
        }
    }
    terminal.enter_cooked_mode()
}
```
Parsing PTY bytes directly does not require opening a terminal handle:

```
use termina::{Event, Parser};
let mut parser = Parser::default();
parser.parse(b"\x1b[5~", false);
assert!(matches!(parser.pop(), Some(Event::Key(_))));
```

# TermwizBackend in ratatui::backend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/backend/struct.TermwizBackend.html

`pub struct TermwizBackend { /* private fields */ }`**crate feature**only.

`termwiz`## Expand description

A [ Backend](https://docs.rs/prelude/backend/index.html) implementation that uses

[Termwiz](https://crates.io/crates/termwiz)to render to the terminal.

The `TermwizBackend` struct is a wrapper around a [ BufferedTerminal](https://docs.rs/termwiz/0.23.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/termwiz/terminal/buffered/struct.BufferedTerminal.html), which is used to send
commands to the terminal. It provides methods for drawing content, manipulating the cursor, and
clearing the terminal screen.

Most applications should not call the methods on `TermwizBackend` directly, but will instead
use the [ Terminal](https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/struct.Terminal.html) struct, which provides a more ergonomic interface.

This backend automatically enables raw mode and switches to the alternate screen when it is
created using the [ TermwizBackend::new](https://docs.rs/struct.TermwizBackend.html#method.new) method (and disables raw mode and returns to the main
screen when dropped). Use the

[to create a new instance with a custom](https://docs.rs/struct.TermwizBackend.html#method.with_buffered_terminal)

`TermwizBackend::with_buffered_terminal`[if this is not desired.](https://docs.rs/termwiz/0.23.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/termwiz/terminal/buffered/struct.BufferedTerminal.html)

`BufferedTerminal`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use ratatui::Terminal;
use ratatui::backend::TermwizBackend;
let backend = TermwizBackend::new()?;
let mut terminal = Terminal::new(backend)?;
terminal.clear()?;
terminal.draw(|frame| {
    // -- snip --
})?;
```
See the [Examples](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/tree/main/ratatui/examples/README.md) directory for more examples. See the [ backend](https://docs.rs/prelude/backend/index.html) module documentation
for more details on raw mode and alternate screen.

# termwiz - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/termwiz/0.23.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/termwiz/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#terminal-wizardry)Terminal Wizardry

This is a rust crate that provides a number of support functions for applications interested in either displaying data to a terminal or in building a terminal emulator.

It is currently in active development and subject to fairly wild sweeping changes.

Included functionality:

- `Surface`models a terminal display and its component- `Cell`s
- Terminal attributes are aware of modern features such as
True Color, [Hyperlinks](https://gist.github.com/egmontkob/eb114294efbcd5adb1944c9f3cb5feda)and will also support sixel and iterm style terminal graphics display.
- `Surface`s include a log of- `Change`s and an API for consuming and applying deltas. This is a powerful building block for synchronizing screen instances.
- Escape sequence parser decodes inscrutable escape sequences and gives them semantic meaning, making the code that uses them clearer. The decoded escapes can be re-encoded, allowing applications to start with the semantic meaning and emit the appropriate escape sequence without embedding obscure binary bytes.
- `Capabilities`allows probing for terminal capabilities that may not be included in the system terminfo database, and overriding them in an embedding application.
- `Terminal`trait provides an abstraction over unix style ttys and Windows style console APIs.- `Change`s from- `Surface`can be rendered to- `Terminal`s.- `Terminal`s allow decoding mouse and keyboard inputs in both blocking or non-blocking mode.
- `Widget`trait allows composition of UI elements at a higher level.
- `LineEditor`provides line editing facilities similar to those in the unix shell.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `widgets`- enables the widget layout and related traits
- `use_serde`- makes a number of structs serde serializable

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.
