## Expand description

[Ratatui Website](https://ratatui.rs/) · [API Docs](https://docs.rs/ratatui) · [Examples](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/tree/main/ratatui/examples/README.md) · [Changelog](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) · [Breaking Changes](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/blob/main/BREAKING-CHANGES.md)

[Contributing](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) · [Report a bug](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/issues/new?labels=bug&projects=&template=bug_report.md) · [Request a Feature](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/issues/new?labels=enhancement&projects=&template=feature_request.md) · [Create a Pull Request](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/compare)

[Ratatui](https://ratatui.rs/) is a crate for cooking up terminal user interfaces in Rust. It is a
lightweight library that provides a set of [widgets](https://docs.rs/widgets/index.html) and utilities to build complex
Rust TUIs. Ratatui was forked from the [tui-rs](https://crates.io/crates/tui) crate in 2023 in order to continue its
development.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

Add `ratatui` and `crossterm` as dependencies to your cargo.toml:

`cargo add ratatui crossterm`Then you can create a simple “Hello World” application:

```
use crossterm::event;
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    ratatui::run(|mut terminal| {
        loop {
            terminal.draw(|frame| frame.render_widget("Hello World!", frame.area()))?;
            if event::read()?.is_key_press() {
                break Ok(());
            }
        }
    })
}
```
The full code for this example which contains a little more detail is in the [Examples](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/tree/main/ratatui/examples/README.md)
directory. For more guidance on different ways to structure your application see the
[Application Patterns](https://ratatui.rs/concepts/application-patterns/) and [Hello Ratatui tutorial](https://ratatui.rs/tutorials/hello-ratatui/) sections in the [Ratatui Website](https://ratatui.rs/) and the
various [Examples](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/tree/main/ratatui/examples/README.md). There are also several starter [Templates](https://ratatui.rs/templates/) available to help you get
started quickly with common patterns.

[§](https://docs.rs#which-setup-path-should-i-use)Which setup path should I use?

Most application authors should start with one of these entry points:

- Use `run()`
- Use `init()``restore()``try_init()``try_restore()`
- Use `init_with_options()``try_init_with_options()``Viewport`

Reach for [ Terminal::new](https://docs.rs/struct.Terminal.html#method.new) or

[directly only when you need custom backend construction or terminal setup that Ratatui’s convenience functions do not manage.](https://docs.rs/struct.Terminal.html#method.with_options)

`Terminal::with_options`[§](https://docs.rs#which-crate-should-i-use)Which crate should I use?

Most application authors should stay in this `ratatui` crate. It is the docs.rs entry point
for building apps and re-exports the pieces most applications need.

Reach for other crates in the workspace only when you specifically need a lower-level layer:

- `ratatui-core`
- `ratatui-widgets`
- `ratatui-crossterm`- `ratatui-termion`- `ratatui-termina`- `ratatui-termwiz`

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-organization)Crate Organization

Starting with Ratatui 0.30.0, the project was reorganized into a modular workspace to improve
compilation times, API stability, and dependency management. Most applications should continue
using this main `ratatui` crate, which re-exports everything for convenience:

- `ratatui`
- `ratatui-core`
- `ratatui-widgets`
- **Backend crates**:- `ratatui-crossterm`- `ratatui-termion`- `ratatui-termina`- `ratatui-termwiz`
- `ratatui-macros`

**For application developers**: `ratatui` remains the recommended starting point.

**For widget library authors**: Consider depending on [ ratatui-core](https://crates.io/crates/ratatui-core) instead of the full

`ratatui` crate for better API stability and reduced dependencies.See [ARCHITECTURE.md](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md) for detailed information about the crate organization and design
decisions.

[§](https://docs.rs#writing-applications)Writing Applications

Ratatui is based on the principle of immediate rendering with intermediate buffers. This means
that for each frame, your app must render all [ widgets](https://docs.rs/widgets/index.html) that are supposed to be part of the
UI. This is in contrast to the retained mode style of rendering where widgets are updated and
then automatically redrawn on the next frame. See the

[Rendering](https://ratatui.rs/concepts/rendering/)section of the

[Ratatui Website](https://ratatui.rs/)for more info.

Ratatui uses [Crossterm](https://crates.io/crates/crossterm) by default as it works on most platforms. See the [Installation](https://ratatui.rs/installation/)
section of the [Ratatui Website](https://ratatui.rs/) for more details on how to use other backends ([Termion](https://crates.io/crates/termion) /
[Termwiz](https://crates.io/crates/termwiz)).

Every application built with `ratatui` needs to implement the following steps:

- Initialize the terminal (see the `init`module
- A main loop that:
- Draws the UI
- Handles input events

- Restore the terminal state

[§](https://docs.rs#initialize-and-restore-the-terminal)Initialize and restore the terminal

The simplest way to initialize and run a terminal application is to use the [ run()](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html) function,
which handles terminal initialization, restoration, and panic hooks automatically:

```
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    ratatui::run(|mut terminal| {
        loop {
            terminal.draw(render)?;
            if should_quit()? {
                break Ok(());
            }
        }
    })
}
fn render(frame: &mut ratatui::Frame) {
    // ...
}
fn should_quit() -> std::io::Result<bool> {
    // ...
}
```
For more control over initialization and restoration, you can use [ init()](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html) and

[:](https://docs.rs/fn.restore.html)

`restore()````
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let mut terminal = ratatui::init();
    let result = run_app(&mut terminal);
    ratatui::restore();
    result
}
fn run_app(terminal: &mut ratatui::DefaultTerminal) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    loop {
        terminal.draw(render)?;
        if should_quit()? {
            break Ok(());
        }
    }
}
```
Use [ run()](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html) as the default. Reach for

[/](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html)

`init()`[when setup and teardown should surround code outside the application closure, and see the](https://docs.rs/fn.restore.html)

`restore()`[documentation for the full chooser including](https://docs.rs/init/index.html)

`init` module`try_*` and `*_with_options`.[§](https://docs.rs#manual-terminal-and-backend-construction)Manual Terminal and Backend Construction

Before the convenience functions were introduced in version 0.28.1 ([ init()](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html)/

[) and 0.30.0 (](https://docs.rs/fn.restore.html)

`restore()`[), applications constructed](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html)

`run()`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Terminal.html)

`Terminal`[instances manually. This approach is still supported for applications that need fine-grained control over initialization, custom backends, or terminal setup that should happen outside Ratatui’s convenience helpers. See the](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.Backend.html)

`Backend`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Terminal.html)

`Terminal`[module documentation for details.](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.Backend.html)

`backend`See the [ backend module](https://docs.rs/backend/index.html) and the

[Backends](https://ratatui.rs/concepts/backends/)section of the

[Ratatui Website](https://ratatui.rs/)for more info on the alternate screen and raw mode. Learn more about different backend options in the

[Backend Comparison](https://ratatui.rs/concepts/backends/comparison/)guide.

[§](https://docs.rs#drawing-the-ui)Drawing the UI

Drawing the UI is done by calling the [ Terminal::draw](https://docs.rs/struct.Terminal.html#method.draw) method on the terminal instance. This
method takes a closure that is called with a

[instance. The](https://docs.rs/struct.Frame.html)

`Frame`[provides the size of the area to draw to and allows the app to render any](https://docs.rs/struct.Frame.html)

`Frame`[using the provided](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html)

`Widget`[method. After this closure returns, a diff is performed and only the changes are drawn to the terminal. See the](https://docs.rs/struct.Frame.html#method.render_widget)

`render_widget`[Widgets](https://ratatui.rs/recipes/widgets/)section of the

[Ratatui Website](https://ratatui.rs/)and the

[Widget Recipes](https://ratatui.rs/recipes/widgets/)for more info on creating effective UIs.

The closure passed to the [ Terminal::draw](https://docs.rs/struct.Terminal.html#method.draw) method should handle the rendering of a full frame.
For guidance on setting up the terminal before drawing, see the

[documentation.](https://docs.rs/init/index.html)

`init` module```
use ratatui::Frame;
use ratatui::widgets::Paragraph;
fn run(terminal: &mut ratatui::DefaultTerminal) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    loop {
        terminal.draw(|frame| render(frame))?;
        if handle_events()? {
            break Ok(());
        }
    }
}
fn render(frame: &mut Frame) {
    let text = Paragraph::new("Hello World!");
    frame.render_widget(text, frame.area());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#what-happens-if)What happens if…

- **If the terminal is resized:**
 Ratatui does not redraw automatically when a resize event arrives. Your app should continue the event loop and call- `Terminal::draw`- `Terminal::resize`
- **If**- `Terminal::try_draw`
 The render pass stops early and Ratatui does not promise that the terminal, cursor, and internal buffers are still synchronized. In most applications, return the error and let the surrounding setup path restore terminal state on exit.
- **If you move the cursor directly:**
 Cursor changes made through backend-specific APIs or- `Terminal`- `Frame`
- **If you mutate the backend directly:**
 Direct backend changes bypass Ratatui’s diffing and viewport bookkeeping. After doing that, run a full draw pass or clear the terminal before assuming Ratatui’s internal view still matches the screen.

[§](https://docs.rs#handling-events)Handling events

Ratatui does not include any input handling. Instead event handling can be implemented by
calling backend library methods directly. See the [Handling Events](https://ratatui.rs/concepts/event-handling/) section of the [Ratatui
Website](https://ratatui.rs/) for conceptual information. For example, if you are using [Crossterm](https://crates.io/crates/crossterm), you can use the
[ crossterm::event](https://docs.rs/crossterm/latest/crossterm/event/index.html) module to handle events.

```
use crossterm::event::{self, Event, KeyCode, KeyEvent, KeyEventKind};
fn handle_events() -> std::io::Result<bool> {
    match event::read()? {
        Event::Key(key) if key.kind == KeyEventKind::Press => match key.code {
            KeyCode::Char('q') => return Ok(true),
            // handle other key events
            _ => {}
        },
        // handle other events
        _ => {}
    }
    Ok(false)
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#layout-1)Layout

The library comes with a basic yet useful layout management object called [ Layout](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Layout.html) which
allows you to split the available space into multiple areas and then render widgets in each
area. This lets you describe a responsive terminal UI by nesting layouts. See the

[Layout](https://ratatui.rs/recipes/layout/)section of the

[Ratatui Website](https://ratatui.rs/)for more info, and check out the

[Layout Recipes](https://ratatui.rs/recipes/layout/)for practical examples.

```
use ratatui::Frame;
use ratatui::layout::{Constraint, Layout};
use ratatui::widgets::Block;
fn draw(frame: &mut Frame) {
    use Constraint::{Fill, Length, Min};
    let vertical = Layout::vertical([Length(1), Min(0), Length(1)]);
    let [title_area, main_area, status_area] = vertical.areas(frame.area());
    let horizontal = Layout::horizontal([Fill(1); 2]);
    let [left_area, right_area] = horizontal.areas(main_area);
    frame.render_widget(Block::bordered().title("Title Bar"), title_area);
    frame.render_widget(Block::bordered().title("Status Bar"), status_area);
    frame.render_widget(Block::bordered().title("Left"), left_area);
    frame.render_widget(Block::bordered().title("Right"), right_area);
}
```
Running this example produces the following output:

```
Title Bar───────────────────────────────────
┌Left────────────────┐┌Right───────────────┐
│                    ││                    │
└────────────────────┘└────────────────────┘
Status Bar──────────────────────────────────
```
[§](https://docs.rs#text-and-styling)Text and styling

The [ Text](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Text.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Line.html)

`Line`[types are the building blocks of the library and are used in many places.](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Span.html)

`Span`[is a list of](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Text.html)

`Text`[s and a](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Line.html)

`Line`[is a list of](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Line.html)

`Line`[s. A](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Span.html)

`Span`[is a string with a specific style.](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Span.html)

`Span`The [ style module](https://docs.rs/style/index.html) provides types that represent the various styling options. The most
important one is

[which represents the foreground and background colors and the text attributes of a](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Style.html)

`Style`[. The](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Span.html)

`Span`[also provides a](https://docs.rs/style/index.html)

`style` module[trait that allows short-hand syntax to apply a style to widgets and text. See the](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Stylize.html)

`Stylize`[Styling Text](https://ratatui.rs/recipes/render/style-text/)section of the

[Ratatui Website](https://ratatui.rs/)for more info, and explore the

[Styling Recipes](https://ratatui.rs/recipes/render/)for creative examples.

```
use ratatui::Frame;
use ratatui::layout::{Constraint, Layout};
use ratatui::style::{Color, Modifier, Style, Stylize};
use ratatui::text::{Line, Span};
use ratatui::widgets::{Block, Paragraph};
fn draw(frame: &mut Frame) {
    let areas = Layout::vertical([Constraint::Length(1); 4]).split(frame.area());
    let line = Line::from(vec![
        Span::raw("Hello "),
        Span::styled(
            "World",
            Style::new()
                .fg(Color::Green)
                .bg(Color::White)
                .add_modifier(Modifier::BOLD),
        ),
        "!".red().on_light_yellow().italic(),
    ]);
    frame.render_widget(line, areas[0]);
    // using the short-hand syntax and implicit conversions
    let paragraph = Paragraph::new("Hello World!".red().on_white().bold());
    frame.render_widget(paragraph, areas[1]);
    // style the whole widget instead of just the text
    let paragraph = Paragraph::new("Hello World!").style(Style::new().red().on_white());
    frame.render_widget(paragraph, areas[2]);
    // use the simpler short-hand syntax
    let paragraph = Paragraph::new("Hello World!").blue().on_yellow();
    frame.render_widget(paragraph, areas[3]);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

The crate provides a set of optional features that can be enabled in your `Cargo.toml` file.

- `default`- `underline-color`feature which allows you to set the underline color of text, the- `macros`feature which provides some useful macros and- `layout-cache`which speeds up layout cache calculations.

Generally an application will only use one backend, so you should only enable one of the following features:

- `crossterm`- *(enabled by default)*— enables the- `CrosstermBackend`- `crossterm`
- `crossterm_0_28`
- `crossterm_0_29`
- `termion`- `TermionBackend`- `termion`
- `termina`- `TerminaBackend`- `termina`
- `termwiz`- `TermwizBackend`- `termwiz`
- `std`- *(enabled by default)*— enables std

The following optional features are available for all backends:

- `serde`- `serde`
- `layout-cache`- *(enabled by default)*— enables layout cache
- `palette`- `palette`- `Color`
- `portable-atomic`
- `scrolling-regions`
- `macros`- *(enabled by default)*— enables the- `macros`
- `all-widgets`- *(enabled by default)*— enables all widgets.

Widgets that add dependencies are gated behind feature flags to prevent unused transitive dependencies. The available features are:

- `widget-calendar`- *(enabled by default)*— enables the- `calendar`

The following optional features are only available for some backends:

- `underline-color`- *(enabled by default)*— Enables the backend code that sets the underline color. Underline color is only supported by the Crossterm, Termina, and Termwiz backends, and is not supported on Windows 7.

The following features are unstable and may change in the future:

-
`unstable`
-
`unstable-rendered-line-info``Paragraph::line_count``Paragraph::line_width`[Issue 293](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/issues/293)for more details.
-
`unstable-widget-ref``WidgetRef``StatefulWidgetRef`
-
`unstable-backend-writer`

# ratatui/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![no_std]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)// show the feature flags in the generated documentation
[3](https://docs.rs#3)#![cfg_attr(docsrs, feature(doc_cfg))]
[4](https://docs.rs#4)#![doc(
[5](https://docs.rs#5)    html_logo_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ratatui/ratatui/main/assets/logo.png",
[6](https://docs.rs#6)    html_favicon_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ratatui/ratatui/main/assets/favicon.ico"
[7](https://docs.rs#7))]
[8](https://docs.rs#8)#![warn(missing_docs)]
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! ![Release header](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/blob/b23480adfa9430697071c906c7ba4d4f9bd37a73/assets/release-header.png?raw=true)
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! <div align="center">
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! [![Crate Badge]][Crate] [![Docs Badge]][API Docs] [![CI Badge]][CI Workflow] [![Deps.rs
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! Badge]][Deps.rs]<br> [![Codecov Badge]][Codecov] [![License Badge]](./LICENSE) [![Sponsors
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! Badge]][GitHub Sponsors]<br> [![Discord Badge]][Discord Server] [![Matrix Badge]][Matrix]
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! [![Forum Badge]][Forum]<br>
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! [Ratatui Website] · [API Docs] · [Examples] · [Changelog] · [Breaking Changes]<br>
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! [Contributing] · [Report a bug] · [Request a Feature] · [Create a Pull Request]
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! </div>
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! [Ratatui][Ratatui Website] is a crate for cooking up terminal user interfaces in Rust. It is a
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! lightweight library that provides a set of [widgets](`widgets`) and utilities to build complex
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! Rust TUIs. Ratatui was forked from the [tui-rs] crate in 2023 in order to continue its
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! development.
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! ## Quickstart
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! Add `ratatui` and `crossterm` as dependencies to your cargo.toml:
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! ```shell
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! cargo add ratatui crossterm
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! ```
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! Then you can create a simple "Hello World" application:
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! ```rust,no_run
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! use crossterm::event;
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!     ratatui::run(|mut terminal| {
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!         loop {
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!             terminal.draw(|frame| frame.render_widget("Hello World!", frame.area()))?;
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!             if event::read()?.is_key_press() {
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!                 break Ok(());
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!             }
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!         }
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!     })
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! }
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ```
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! The full code for this example which contains a little more detail is in the [Examples]
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! directory. For more guidance on different ways to structure your application see the
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! [Application Patterns] and [Hello Ratatui tutorial] sections in the [Ratatui Website] and the
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! various [Examples]. There are also several starter [Templates] available to help you get
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! started quickly with common patterns.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! ## Which setup path should I use?
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! Most application authors should start with one of these entry points:
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! - Use [`run()`] for normal applications. It initializes the terminal, runs your app, and
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!   restores the terminal on exit.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! - Use [`init()`] / [`restore()`] (or [`try_init()`] / [`try_restore()`]) when you want manual
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!   control over terminal lifetime and the event loop structure.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! - Use [`init_with_options()`] / [`try_init_with_options()`] when you need a custom [`Viewport`],
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!   such as inline rendering or a fixed drawing region.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! Reach for [`Terminal::new`] or [`Terminal::with_options`] directly only when you need custom
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! backend construction or terminal setup that Ratatui's convenience functions do not manage.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! ## Which crate should I use?
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! Most application authors should stay in this `ratatui` crate. It is the docs.rs entry point
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! for building apps and re-exports the pieces most applications need.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! Reach for other crates in the workspace only when you specifically need a lower-level layer:
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! - [`ratatui-core`] for widget libraries, custom integrations, and lower-level rendering
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!   contracts
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! - [`ratatui-widgets`] when you only need the built-in widgets crate as a dependency
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! - [`ratatui-crossterm`], [`ratatui-termion`], [`ratatui-termina`], or [`ratatui-termwiz`] when
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!   your application needs backend-specific APIs or a direct backend dependency
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! # Other documentation
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! - [Ratatui Website] - explains the library's concepts and provides step-by-step tutorials
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! - [Tutorials] - step-by-step guides including [Hello Ratatui tutorial] and [Counter App]
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! - [Recipes] - practical how-to guides for common tasks and patterns
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! - [FAQ] - frequently asked questions and answers
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! - [Templates] - pre-built project templates using [Cargo Generate]
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! - [Showcase] - a gallery of applications and widgets built with Ratatui
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! - [Ratatui Forum][Forum] - a place to ask questions and discuss the library
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! - [API Docs] - the full API documentation for the library on docs.rs.
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! - [Examples] - a collection of examples that demonstrate how to use the library.
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! - [Contributing] - Please read this if you are interested in contributing to the project.
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! - [Changelog] - generated by [git-cliff] utilizing [Conventional Commits].
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! - [Breaking Changes] - a list of breaking changes in the library.
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! You can also watch the [FOSDEM 2024 talk] about Ratatui which gives a brief introduction to
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! terminal user interfaces and showcases the features of Ratatui, along with a hello world demo.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! ## Getting Help
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! If you need help or have questions, check out our [FAQ] for common questions and solutions.

[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! # Crate Organization
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! Starting with Ratatui 0.30.0, the project was reorganized into a modular workspace to improve
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! compilation times, API stability, and dependency management. Most applications should continue
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! using this main `ratatui` crate, which re-exports everything for convenience:
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! - **[`ratatui`](crate)**: Main crate with complete functionality (recommended for apps)
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! - **[`ratatui-core`]**: Core traits and types for widget libraries
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! - **[`ratatui-widgets`]**: Built-in widget implementations
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! - **Backend crates**: [`ratatui-crossterm`], [`ratatui-termion`], [`ratatui-termina`],
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!   [`ratatui-termwiz`]
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! - **[`ratatui-macros`]**: Macros for simplifying the boilerplate
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! **For application developers**: `ratatui` remains the recommended starting point.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! **For widget library authors**: Consider depending on [`ratatui-core`] instead of the full
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! `ratatui` crate for better API stability and reduced dependencies.
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! See [ARCHITECTURE.md] for detailed information about the crate organization and design
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! decisions.
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! # Writing Applications
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! Ratatui is based on the principle of immediate rendering with intermediate buffers. This means
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! that for each frame, your app must render all [`widgets`] that are supposed to be part of the
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! UI. This is in contrast to the retained mode style of rendering where widgets are updated and
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! then automatically redrawn on the next frame. See the [Rendering] section of the [Ratatui
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! Website] for more info.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! Ratatui uses [Crossterm] by default as it works on most platforms. See the [Installation]
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! section of the [Ratatui Website] for more details on how to use other backends ([Termion] /
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! [Termwiz]).
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! Every application built with `ratatui` needs to implement the following steps:
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! - Initialize the terminal (see the [`init` module] for convenient initialization functions)
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! - A main loop that:
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!   - Draws the UI
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!   - Handles input events
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! - Restore the terminal state
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! ## Initialize and restore the terminal
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! The simplest way to initialize and run a terminal application is to use the [`run()`] function,
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! which handles terminal initialization, restoration, and panic hooks automatically:
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! ```rust,no_run
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!     ratatui::run(|mut terminal| {
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!         loop {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!             terminal.draw(render)?;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!             if should_quit()? {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!                 break Ok(());
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!             }
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!         }
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!     })
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! }
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! fn render(frame: &mut ratatui::Frame) {
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!     // ...
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! }
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//!
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! fn should_quit() -> std::io::Result<bool> {
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//!     // ...
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! #   Ok(false)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! }
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! ```
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! For more control over initialization and restoration, you can use [`init()`] and [`restore()`]:
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! ```rust,no_run
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!     let mut terminal = ratatui::init();
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!     let result = run_app(&mut terminal);
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!     ratatui::restore();
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!     result
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! }
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! fn run_app(terminal: &mut ratatui::DefaultTerminal) -> std::io::Result<()> {
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!     loop {
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!         terminal.draw(render)?;
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!         if should_quit()? {
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!             break Ok(());
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//!         }
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!     }
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! }
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! # fn render(_frame: &mut ratatui::Frame) {}
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! # fn should_quit() -> std::io::Result<bool> { Ok(false) }
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! ```
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! Use [`run()`] as the default. Reach for [`init()`] / [`restore()`] when setup and teardown
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! should surround code outside the application closure, and see the [`init` module] documentation
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! for the full chooser including `try_*` and `*_with_options`.
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//!
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! ### Manual Terminal and Backend Construction
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! Before the convenience functions were introduced in version 0.28.1 ([`init()`]/[`restore()`])
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! and 0.30.0 ([`run()`]), applications constructed [`Terminal`] and [`Backend`] instances
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! manually. This approach is still supported for applications that need fine-grained control over
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! initialization, custom backends, or terminal setup that should happen outside Ratatui's
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! convenience helpers. See the [`Terminal`] and [`backend`] module documentation for details.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//!
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! See the [`backend` module] and the [Backends] section of the [Ratatui Website] for more info on
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! the alternate screen and raw mode. Learn more about different backend options in the [Backend
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! Comparison] guide.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//!
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! ## Drawing the UI
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! Drawing the UI is done by calling the [`Terminal::draw`] method on the terminal instance. This
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! method takes a closure that is called with a [`Frame`] instance. The [`Frame`] provides the size
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! of the area to draw to and allows the app to render any [`Widget`] using the provided
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! [`render_widget`] method. After this closure returns, a diff is performed and only the changes
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! are drawn to the terminal. See the [Widgets] section of the [Ratatui Website] and the [Widget
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! Recipes] for more info on creating effective UIs.
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//!
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! The closure passed to the [`Terminal::draw`] method should handle the rendering of a full frame.
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! For guidance on setting up the terminal before drawing, see the [`init` module] documentation.
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! ```rust,no_run
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! use ratatui::Frame;
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! use ratatui::widgets::Paragraph;
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! fn run(terminal: &mut ratatui::DefaultTerminal) -> std::io::Result<()> {
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!     loop {
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!         terminal.draw(|frame| render(frame))?;
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!         if handle_events()? {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!             break Ok(());
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!         }
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//!     }
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! fn render(frame: &mut Frame) {
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!     let text = Paragraph::new("Hello World!");
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!     frame.render_widget(text, frame.area());
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! # fn handle_events() -> std::io::Result<bool> { Ok(false) }
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! ```
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! ### What happens if...
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! - **If the terminal is resized:**<br> Ratatui does not redraw automatically when a resize event
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//!   arrives. Your app should continue the event loop and call [`Terminal::draw`] again. During
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//!   that render pass, Ratatui checks the backend's current size instead of assuming the resize
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!   events were complete or up to date. This keeps layout based on the size that actually exists
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//!   when rendering, even if multiple resize events were coalesced, missed, or delivered before the
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!   UI redraws. Fullscreen and inline viewports update their internal size during that render
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!   pass; fixed viewports keep their configured rectangle until you call [`Terminal::resize`].
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! - **If [`Terminal::try_draw`] returns an error:**<br> The render pass stops early and Ratatui
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!   does not promise that the terminal, cursor, and internal buffers are still synchronized. In
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//!   most applications, return the error and let the surrounding setup path restore terminal state
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!   on exit.
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! - **If you move the cursor directly:**<br> Cursor changes made through backend-specific APIs or
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!   [`Terminal`] cursor methods can be overwritten by the next render pass if that pass sets
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!   cursor state through [`Frame`]. Prefer choosing one path and using it consistently.
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! - **If you mutate the backend directly:**<br> Direct backend changes bypass Ratatui's diffing
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//!   and viewport bookkeeping. After doing that, run a full draw pass or clear the terminal before
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!   assuming Ratatui's internal view still matches the screen.
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//!
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! ## Handling events
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! Ratatui does not include any input handling. Instead event handling can be implemented by
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! calling backend library methods directly. See the [Handling Events] section of the [Ratatui
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! Website] for conceptual information. For example, if you are using [Crossterm], you can use the
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! [`crossterm::event`] module to handle events.
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//!
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! ```rust,no_run
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! use crossterm::event::{self, Event, KeyCode, KeyEvent, KeyEventKind};
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//!
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! fn handle_events() -> std::io::Result<bool> {
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!     match event::read()? {
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!         Event::Key(key) if key.kind == KeyEventKind::Press => match key.code {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!             KeyCode::Char('q') => return Ok(true),
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//!             // handle other key events
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//!             _ => {}
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//!         },
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//!         // handle other events
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!         _ => {}
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//!     }
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//!     Ok(false)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! }
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! ```
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//!
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! ## Layout
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! The library comes with a basic yet useful layout management object called [`Layout`] which
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! allows you to split the available space into multiple areas and then render widgets in each
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! area. This lets you describe a responsive terminal UI by nesting layouts. See the [Layout]
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//! section of the [Ratatui Website] for more info, and check out the [Layout Recipes] for
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! practical examples.
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//!
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! ```rust,no_run
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! use ratatui::Frame;
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! use ratatui::layout::{Constraint, Layout};
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! use ratatui::widgets::Block;
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! fn draw(frame: &mut Frame) {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//!     use Constraint::{Fill, Length, Min};
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//!     let vertical = Layout::vertical([Length(1), Min(0), Length(1)]);
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//!     let [title_area, main_area, status_area] = vertical.areas(frame.area());
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//!     let horizontal = Layout::horizontal([Fill(1); 2]);
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//!     let [left_area, right_area] = horizontal.areas(main_area);
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//!
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//!     frame.render_widget(Block::bordered().title("Title Bar"), title_area);
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//!     frame.render_widget(Block::bordered().title("Status Bar"), status_area);
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!     frame.render_widget(Block::bordered().title("Left"), left_area);
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//!     frame.render_widget(Block::bordered().title("Right"), right_area);
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//! }
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//! ```
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//!
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//! Running this example produces the following output:
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//!
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//! ```text
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//! Title Bar───────────────────────────────────
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//! ┌Left────────────────┐┌Right───────────────┐
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//! │                    ││                    │
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//! └────────────────────┘└────────────────────┘
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//! Status Bar──────────────────────────────────
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//! ```
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//! ## Text and styling
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//!
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//! The [`Text`], [`Line`] and [`Span`] types are the building blocks of the library and are used in
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//! many places. [`Text`] is a list of [`Line`]s and a [`Line`] is a list of [`Span`]s. A [`Span`]
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//! is a string with a specific style.
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//!
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//! The [`style` module] provides types that represent the various styling options. The most
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//! important one is [`Style`] which represents the foreground and background colors and the text
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//! attributes of a [`Span`]. The [`style` module] also provides a [`Stylize`] trait that allows
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! short-hand syntax to apply a style to widgets and text. See the [Styling Text] section of the
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//! [Ratatui Website] for more info, and explore the [Styling Recipes] for creative examples.
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//!
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//! ```rust,no_run
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//! use ratatui::Frame;
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//! use ratatui::layout::{Constraint, Layout};
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//! use ratatui::style::{Color, Modifier, Style, Stylize};
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//! use ratatui::text::{Line, Span};
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//! use ratatui::widgets::{Block, Paragraph};
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//!
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//! fn draw(frame: &mut Frame) {
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//!     let areas = Layout::vertical([Constraint::Length(1); 4]).split(frame.area());
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//!
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!     let line = Line::from(vec![
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//!         Span::raw("Hello "),
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//!         Span::styled(
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//!             "World",
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//!             Style::new()
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//!                 .fg(Color::Green)
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//!                 .bg(Color::White)
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//!                 .add_modifier(Modifier::BOLD),
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//!         ),
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//!         "!".red().on_light_yellow().italic(),
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//!     ]);
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//!     frame.render_widget(line, areas[0]);
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//!
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//!     // using the short-hand syntax and implicit conversions
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//!     let paragraph = Paragraph::new("Hello World!".red().on_white().bold());
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//!     frame.render_widget(paragraph, areas[1]);
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//!
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//!     // style the whole widget instead of just the text
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//!     let paragraph = Paragraph::new("Hello World!").style(Style::new().red().on_white());
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//!     frame.render_widget(paragraph, areas[2]);
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//!
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//!     // use the simpler short-hand syntax
[374](https://docs.rs#374)//!     let paragraph = Paragraph::new("Hello World!").blue().on_yellow();
[375](https://docs.rs#375)//!     frame.render_widget(paragraph, areas[3]);
[376](https://docs.rs#376)//! }
[377](https://docs.rs#377)//! ```

# ratatui::widgets - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/0.30.2/ratatui/widgets/index.html

## Expand description

Widgets are the building blocks of user interfaces in Ratatui.

They are used to create and manage the layout and style of the terminal interface. Widgets can be combined and nested to create complex UIs, and can be easily customized to suit the needs of your application.

Ratatui provides a wide variety of built-in widgets that can be used to quickly create UIs.
Additionally, [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html),

[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

`&str`[,](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Span.html)

`Span`[, and](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Line.html)

`Line`[can be used as widgets (though often](https://docs.rs/prelude/struct.Text.html)

`Text`[is used instead of these directly as it allows wrapping and surrounding the text with a block).](https://docs.rs/struct.Paragraph.html)

`Paragraph`[§](https://docs.rs#crate-organization)Crate Organization

Starting with Ratatui 0.30.0, the project was split into multiple crates for better modularity:

- `ratatui-core`- `Widget`- `StatefulWidget`- `String`- `&str`- `Span`- `Line`- `Text`
- `ratatui-widgets`- `Block`- `Paragraph`- `List`
- `ratatui`- `WidgetRef`- `StatefulWidgetRef`- `ratatui`crate as they are experimental.

This split serves different user needs:

- **App Authors**: Most application developers should use the main- `ratatui`
- **Widget Library Authors**: When creating third-party widget libraries, consider depending only on- `ratatui-core`
- **Minimalist Projects**: Use- `ratatui-core`

The modular structure allows widget library authors to create lightweight dependencies while still being compatible with the broader Ratatui ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-widgets)Built-in Widgets

Ratatui provides a comprehensive set of built-in widgets:

- `Block`
- `BarChart`
- `calendar::Monthly`
- `Canvas`
- `Chart`
- `Clear`
- `Fill`
- `Gauge`
- `LineGauge`
- `List`
- `Paragraph`
- `Scrollbar`
- `Sparkline`
- `Table`
- `Tabs`
- `RatatuiLogo`
- `RatatuiMascot`

Additionally, primitive text types implement [ Widget](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html):

- `String`
- `&str`
- `Line`
- `Span`
- `Text`

For more information on these widgets, you can view the widget showcase and examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#third-party-widgets)Third-Party Widgets

Beyond the built-in widgets, there’s a rich ecosystem of third-party widgets available that extend Ratatui’s functionality. These community-contributed widgets provide specialized UI components for various use cases.

To discover third-party widgets:

- **Search crates.io**: Look for crates with “tui” or “ratatui” in their names or descriptions
- **Awesome Ratatui**: Check the- [Awesome Ratatui](https://github.com/ratatui-org/awesome-ratatui)repository for a curated list of widgets, libraries, and applications
- **Widget Showcase**: Browse the- [third-party widgets showcase](https://ratatui.rs/showcase/third-party-widgets/)on the Ratatui website to see widgets in action

These third-party widgets cover a wide range of functionality including specialized input components, data visualization widgets, layout helpers, and domain-specific UI elements.

[§](https://docs.rs#widget-traits)Widget Traits

In Ratatui, widgets are implemented as Rust traits, which allow for easy implementation and extension. The main traits for widgets are:

- `Widget`
- `StatefulWidget`
- `WidgetRef`
- `StatefulWidgetRef`

[§](https://docs.rs#widget)`Widget`

The [ Widget](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html) trait is the most basic trait for widgets in Ratatui. It provides the basic
functionality for rendering a widget onto a buffer. Widgets implementing this trait are consumed
when rendered.

```
pub trait Widget {
    fn render(self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer);
}
```
Prior to Ratatui 0.26.0, widgets were generally created for each frame as they were consumed
during rendering. This meant that they were not meant to be stored but used as *commands* to
draw common figures in the UI. Starting with 0.26.0, implementing widgets on references became
the preferred pattern for reusability.

[§](https://docs.rs#statefulwidget)`StatefulWidget`

The [ StatefulWidget](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.StatefulWidget.html) trait is similar to the

[trait, but also includes state that can be managed and updated during rendering. This is useful for widgets that need to remember things between draw calls, such as scroll position or selection state.](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html)

`Widget````
pub trait StatefulWidget {
    type State;
    fn render(self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer, state: &mut Self::State);
}
```
For example, the built-in [ List](https://docs.rs/struct.List.html) widget can highlight the currently selected item. This
requires maintaining an offset to ensure the selected item is visible within the viewport.
Without state, the widget could only provide basic scrolling behavior, but with access to the
previous offset, it can implement natural scrolling where the offset is preserved until the
selected item moves out of view.

[§](https://docs.rs#widgetref-and-statefulwidgetref)`WidgetRef` and `StatefulWidgetRef`

The [ WidgetRef](https://docs.rs/trait.WidgetRef.html) and

[traits were introduced in Ratatui 0.26.0 to enable rendering widgets by reference instead of consuming them. These traits address several important use cases that the original](https://docs.rs/trait.StatefulWidgetRef.html)

`StatefulWidgetRef``Widget` and `StatefulWidget` traits couldn’t handle elegantly.```
pub trait WidgetRef {
    fn render_ref(&self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer);
}
pub trait StatefulWidgetRef {
    type State;
    fn render_ref(&self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer, state: &mut Self::State);
}
```
The reference-based traits solve several key problems:

- **Reusability**: Widgets can be rendered multiple times without being consumed
- **Collections**: Store heterogeneous widgets in collections like- `Vec<Box<dyn WidgetRef>>`
- **Borrowing**: Render widgets when you only have a reference, not ownership
- **Efficiency**: Avoid unnecessary cloning or reconstruction for repeated renders

These traits are currently **experimental** and gated behind the `unstable-widget-ref` feature
flag. This means:

- The API may change in future releases
- Method names, signatures, or behavior might be adjusted based on community feedback
- You must explicitly enable the feature flag to use them: `features = ["unstable-widget-ref"]`
- They are not covered by semantic versioning guarantees until stabilized

The traits are being evaluated for potential breaking changes and improvements. See the
[tracking issue](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/issues/1287) for ongoing discussions and
design considerations.

[§](https://docs.rs#rendering-widgets)Rendering Widgets

Widgets are typically rendered using the [ Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.Frame.html) type, which provides methods for rendering
both consuming and reference-based widgets. These methods are usually called from the closure
passed to

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Terminal.html#method.draw)

`Terminal::draw`[§](https://docs.rs#rendering-consuming-widgets)Rendering Consuming Widgets

Most widgets in Ratatui are rendered using `Frame::render_widget()`, which consumes the widget
when rendering. This is the standard approach for stateless widgets that don’t need to persist
data between frames.

```
terminal.draw(|frame| {
    let widget = Paragraph::new("Hello, world!");
    frame.render_widget(widget, frame.area());
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rendering-widget-references)Rendering Widget References

When you implement widgets on references (`Widget for &MyWidget`), you can render them directly
using the same `Frame::render_widget()` method. This approach enables widget reuse without
reconstruction and is the recommended pattern for new widgets.

```
// Create the widget outside the draw closure
let paragraph = Paragraph::new("Hello, world!").block(Block::bordered());
terminal.draw(|frame| {
    // Widget can be rendered by reference without being consumed
    frame.render_widget(¶graph, frame.area());
});
// The widget can be used again in subsequent frames
terminal.draw(|frame| {
    frame.render_widget(¶graph, frame.area());
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rendering-stateful-widgets)Rendering Stateful Widgets

Widgets that need to maintain state between frames use `Frame::render_stateful_widget()`. This
method takes both the widget and a mutable reference to its state, allowing the widget to read
and modify state during rendering (such as updating scroll positions or handling selections).

```
let mut list_state = ListState::default();
terminal.draw(|frame| {
    let items = vec![ListItem::new("Item 1"), ListItem::new("Item 2")];
    let list = List::new(items);
    frame.render_stateful_widget(list, frame.area(), &mut list_state);
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#single-root-widget-pattern)Single Root Widget Pattern

A common compositional pattern in Ratatui applications is to have a single root widget (often an
`App` struct) that represents your entire application state. This widget is passed to
`Frame::render_widget()`, and within its render method, it calls render on child widgets
directly. This pattern provides a clean separation between your application logic and rendering
code, and allows for easy composition of complex UIs from simpler components.

```
#[derive(Default)]
struct App {
    should_quit: bool,
}
impl Widget for &App {
    fn render(self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer) {
        // Render header
        let header = Paragraph::new("My App").block(Block::bordered());
        header.render(Rect::new(area.x, area.y, area.width, 3), buf);
        // Render main content
        let content = Paragraph::new("Main content area");
        content.render(
            Rect::new(area.x, area.y + 3, area.width, area.height - 3),
            buf,
        );
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#authoring-custom-widgets)Authoring Custom Widgets

When implementing custom widgets in Ratatui, you’ll make fundamental decisions about how your widget manages state and how it’s used by applications. Understanding these choices will help you create widgets that fit well into your application’s architecture. Widget implementation involves several key architectural decisions that work together to determine how your widget behaves - these decisions are independent but complementary, allowing you to mix and match approaches based on your specific needs.

**State Management**: The first choice is where state lives. Some widgets need to track
information between renders - things like scroll positions, selections, or counters. You can
either build this state into the widget itself (widget-owned state) or keep it separate and pass
it in during rendering (external state).

**Ownership Model**: The second choice is how the widget is consumed. Widgets can either be
consumed when rendered (taking ownership) or work by reference (borrowing). Reference-based
widgets can be stored and reused across multiple frames, while consuming widgets are created
fresh each time.

** StatefulWidget vs Mutable References**: When your widget needs state, you have two main
approaches. The

[trait represents the established pattern - it separates the widget from its state, allowing the application to own and manage the state independently. This is what you’ll see in most existing Ratatui code and built-in widgets like](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.StatefulWidget.html)

`StatefulWidget`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.List.html)

`List`[. The mutable reference approach (](https://docs.rs/struct.Table.html)

`Table``Widget for &mut MyWidget`) is newer and less common,
but useful when the state is intrinsic to the widget’s identity. With mutable references, the
widget owns its state directly.The key question for state management is: “If I recreate this widget, should the state reset?”
If yes (like a counter that should start at zero), use mutable references with widget-owned
state. If no (like a list selection that should persist), use [ StatefulWidget](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.StatefulWidget.html) with external
state that the application manages.

**Evolution and Current Recommendations**: Ratatui’s patterns have evolved significantly. Before
version 0.26.0, widgets were typically consuming (`Widget for MyWidget`) and created fresh each
frame. Starting with 0.26.0, reference-based widgets (`Widget for &MyWidget`) became possible,
allowing widgets to be stored and reused. You’ll encounter both patterns in existing code, but
reference-based implementations are now recommended for new widgets because they enable
reusability and automatic [ WidgetRef](https://docs.rs/trait.WidgetRef.html) support through blanket implementations.

For new widgets, implement [ Widget](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html) or

[on references to your widget types (](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.StatefulWidget.html)

`StatefulWidget``&MyWidget` or `&mut MyWidget`). This provides reusability and automatic [support. You can optionally implement the consuming version for backward compatibility.](https://docs.rs/trait.WidgetRef.html)

`WidgetRef`[§](https://docs.rs#state-management-patterns)State Management Patterns

For a comprehensive exploration of different approaches to handling both mutable and immutable
state in widgets, see the [state examples](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/tree/main/examples/concepts/state) in the Ratatui repository. These examples demonstrate
various patterns including:

**Immutable State Patterns** (recommended for most use cases):

- Function-based immutable state (`fn render(frame: &mut Frame, area: Rect, state: &State)`)
- Shared reference widgets (`impl Widget for &MyWidget`)
- Consuming widgets (`impl Widget for MyWidget`)

**Mutable State Patterns** (for widgets that modify state during rendering):

- Function-based mutable state (`fn render(frame: &mut Frame, area: Rect, state: &mut State)`)
- Mutable widget references (`impl Widget for &mut MyWidget`)
- `StatefulWidget`pattern (- `impl StatefulWidget for MyWidget`)
- Custom component traits (`trait MyComponent { fn render(&mut self, frame: &mut Frame, area: Rect) }`)
- Interior mutability with `RefCell`(`struct MyWidget { state: Rc<RefCell<State>> }`)
- Lifetime-based mutable references (`struct MyWidget<'a> { state: &'a mut State }`)
- Nested widget hierarchies (compositions with owned or external state)

Each pattern has different trade-offs in terms of complexity, performance, and architectural fit, making them suitable for different use cases and application designs. For most applications, start with immutable patterns as they are simpler to reason about and less prone to borrowing issues.

[§](https://docs.rs#shared-references-widget)Shared References (`&Widget`)

The recommended pattern for most new widgets implements [ Widget](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html) on a shared reference,
allowing the widget to be rendered multiple times without being consumed. This approach is ideal
for immutable widgets that don’t need to modify their internal state during rendering, and it’s
the most common pattern you should use for new widgets.

```
struct MyWidget {
    content: String,
}
impl Widget for &MyWidget {
    fn render(self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer) {
        Line::raw(&self.content).render(area, buf);
    }
}
```
This automatically provides [ WidgetRef](https://docs.rs/trait.WidgetRef.html) support through blanket implementations and enables
widgets to be stored and reused across frames without reconstruction. For most use cases where
the widget doesn’t need to change its internal state during rendering, this is the best choice.

[§](https://docs.rs#mutable-references-mut-widget)Mutable References (`&mut Widget`)

For widgets that need to modify their internal state during rendering, implement [ Widget](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html) on a
mutable reference. This is a newer pattern that’s less common but useful when the state is
intrinsic to the widget’s identity and behavior. Use this pattern when the widget should own and
manage its state directly, rather than having external state passed in.

```
struct CounterWidget {
    count: u32, // This state belongs to the widget
    label: String,
}
impl Widget for &mut CounterWidget {
    fn render(self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer) {
        self.count += 1; // State changes as part of rendering behavior
        let text = format!("{label}: {count}", label = self.label, count = self.count);
        Line::raw(text).render(area, buf);
    }
}
```
This pattern works well when the widget owns its state and the state is part of the widget’s identity. It’s ideal for counters, animations, cursors, progress indicators, or other widget-specific behavior where the state should reset when you create a new widget instance.

[§](https://docs.rs#consuming-widget-implementation)Consuming Widget Implementation

The consuming widget pattern was the original approach in Ratatui and remains very common in existing codebases. You’ll encounter this pattern frequently when reading examples and community code. Widgets implementing this pattern take ownership when rendered, which means they’re consumed on each use. While not the recommended approach for new widgets, it’s still useful to understand this pattern for compatibility and when working with existing code.

```
struct GreetingWidget {
    name: String,
}
impl Widget for GreetingWidget {
    fn render(self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer) {
        let hello = Span::raw("Hello, ");
        let name = Span::styled(self.name, Modifier::BOLD);
        let line = Line::from(vec![hello, name]);
        line.render(area, buf);
    }
}
```
This approach is simpler and works well for widgets created fresh each frame, but it means the widget cannot be reused. Before reference-based widgets were introduced in version 0.26.0, this was the standard pattern, and it’s still valid for simple use cases or when following existing code patterns.

The easiest way to implement this pattern when you have a reference-based widget is to implement the consuming version on the owned type, which can then call the reference-based implementation:

```
impl Widget for GreetingWidget {
    fn render(self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer) {
        // Call the reference-based implementation
        (&self).render(area, buf);
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#statefulwidget-implementation)`StatefulWidget` Implementation

When your widget needs to work with external state - data that exists independently of the
widget and should persist between widget instances - implement [ StatefulWidget](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.StatefulWidget.html). This is the
established pattern used by built-in widgets like

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.List.html)

`List`[, where the widget configuration is separate from application state like selections or scroll positions.](https://docs.rs/struct.Table.html)

`Table`Like [ Widget](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html), you can implement

[on references to allow reuse, though it’s more common to see this trait implemented on owned types which are consumed during rendering.](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.StatefulWidget.html)

`StatefulWidget````
struct ListView {
    items: Vec<String>,
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct ListState {
    selected: Option<usize>, // This is application state
    scroll_offset: usize,
}
impl StatefulWidget for ListView {
    type State = ListState;
    fn render(self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer, state: &mut ListState) {
        // Render based on external state, possibly modify for scrolling
        let display_text = state
            .selected
            .and_then(|i| self.items.get(i))
            .map_or("None selected", |s| s.as_str());
        Line::raw(display_text).render(area, buf);
    }
}
```
This pattern is ideal for selections, scroll positions, form data, or any state that should persist between renders or be shared across your application. The state exists independently of the widget, so recreating the widget doesn’t reset the state.

[§](https://docs.rs#automatic-widgetref-support)Automatic `WidgetRef` Support

When you implement `Widget for &MyWidget`, you automatically get [ WidgetRef](https://docs.rs/trait.WidgetRef.html) support without
any additional code. Ratatui provides blanket implementations that automatically implement these
traits for any type that implements

[or](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html)

`Widget`[on a reference. This means that implementing](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.StatefulWidget.html)

`StatefulWidget``Widget for &MyWidget` gives you both the standard widget functionality and
the unstable [capabilities for free.](https://docs.rs/trait.WidgetRef.html)

`WidgetRef`[§](https://docs.rs#manual-widgetref-implementation-advanced)Manual `WidgetRef` Implementation (Advanced)

Manual implementation of [ WidgetRef](https://docs.rs/trait.WidgetRef.html) or

[is only necessary when you need to store widgets as trait objects (](https://docs.rs/trait.StatefulWidgetRef.html)

`StatefulWidgetRef``Box<dyn WidgetRef>`) or when you want a different API than
the reference-based [implementation provides. In most cases, the automatic implementation via blanket implementations is sufficient.](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html)

`Widget`These traits enable several benefits:

- Widgets can be stored and rendered multiple times without reconstruction
- Collections of widgets with different types can be stored using `Box<dyn WidgetRef>`
- Avoids the consumption model while maintaining backward compatibility

Manual implementation is only needed when you want to use trait objects or need a different API
than the reference-based [ Widget](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Widget.html) implementation:

```
struct GreetingWidget {
    name: String,
}
// Manual WidgetRef implementation (usually not needed)
impl WidgetRef for GreetingWidget {
    fn render_ref(&self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer) {
        let hello = Span::raw("Hello, ");
        let name = Span::styled(&self.name, Modifier::BOLD);
        let line = Line::from(vec![hello, name]);
        line.render(area, buf);
    }
}
// For backward compatibility
impl Widget for GreetingWidget {
    fn render(self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer) {
        self.render_ref(area, buf);
    }
}
```
This pattern allows the widget to be stored and rendered multiple times:

```
struct App {
    greeting: GreetingWidget,
}
// The widget can be rendered multiple times without reconstruction
fn render_app(app: &App, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer) {
    app.greeting.render_ref(area, buf);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-trait-objects-for-dynamic-collections)Using Trait Objects for Dynamic Collections

The main benefit of manual [ WidgetRef](https://docs.rs/trait.WidgetRef.html) implementation is the ability to create collections of
different widget types using trait objects. This is useful when you need to store widgets with
types that are not known at compile time:

```
let widgets: Vec<Box<dyn WidgetRef>> = vec![Box::new(Greeting), Box::new(Farewell)];
for widget in &widgets {
    widget.render_ref(area, buf);
}
```
However, if you implement `Widget for &MyWidget`, you can achieve similar functionality by
storing references or using the automatic [ WidgetRef](https://docs.rs/trait.WidgetRef.html) implementation without needing to
manually implement the trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#authoring-custom-widget-libraries)Authoring Custom Widget Libraries

When creating a library of custom widgets for distribution, there are specific considerations that will make your library more compatible and accessible to a wider range of users. Following these guidelines will help ensure your widget library works well in various environments and can be easily integrated into different types of applications.

[§](https://docs.rs#depend-on-ratatui_core)Depend on `ratatui_core`

For widget libraries, depend on [ ratatui-core](https://crates.io/crates/ratatui-core) instead of the full

`ratatui` crate. This
provides all the essential types and traits needed for widget development while avoiding
unnecessary dependencies on backends and other components that widget libraries don’t need.This approach offers several key advantages for both library authors and users:

- **Lighter dependencies**: Users don’t pull in backend code they don’t need, keeping their dependency tree smaller and more focused
- **Better compile times**: Fewer dependencies mean faster builds for both development and end-user projects
- **Future-proofing**: Your library remains compatible as Ratatui evolves its architecture, since core widget functionality is stable across versions

[§](https://docs.rs#make-your-crate-no_std-compatible)Make Your Crate `no_std` Compatible

For maximum compatibility, especially in embedded environments, consider making your widget
library `no_std` compatible. This is often easier than you might expect and broadens the range
of projects that can use your widgets.

For more detail on advantages of this, maintenance tips and feature flags, see the
[no-std concept guide](https://ratatui.rs/concepts/no-std/).

To implement `no_std` compatibility, add the `#![no_std]` attribute at the top of your `lib.rs`.
When working in a `no_std` environment, you’ll need to make a few adjustments:

- Use `core::`instead of`std::`for basic functionality
- Add `extern crate alloc;`to access allocation types
- Use `alloc::`for heap-allocated types like`String`,`Vec`, and`Box`

Here’s a complete example of a `no_std` compatible widget:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#![no_std]
extern crate alloc;
use alloc::string::String;
use ratatui_core::buffer::Buffer;
use ratatui_core::layout::Rect;
use ratatui_core::text::Line;
use ratatui_core::widgets::Widget;
struct MyWidget {
    content: String,
}
impl Widget for &MyWidget {
    fn render(self, area: Rect, buf: &mut Buffer) {
        Line::raw(&self.content).render(area, buf);
    }
}
```
The benefits of `no_std` compatibility include:

- **Broader compatibility**: Your widgets work seamlessly in embedded environments and other- `no_std`contexts where standard library functionality isn’t available
- **Easy to adopt**: Even if you haven’t worked with- `no_std`development before, the changes are typically minimal for widget libraries. Most widget logic involves basic data manipulation and rendering operations that work well within- `no_std`constraints, making this compatibility straightforward to implement

# run in ratatui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/0.30.2/ratatui/fn.run.html

`pub fn run<F, R>(f: F) -> R`**crate feature**only.

`crossterm`## Expand description

Run a closure with a terminal initialized with reasonable defaults for most applications.

This function creates a new [ DefaultTerminal](https://docs.rs/type.DefaultTerminal.html) with

[and then runs the given closure with a mutable reference to the terminal. After the closure completes, the terminal is restored to its original state with](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html)

`init`[.](https://docs.rs/fn.restore.html)

`restore`This function is a convenience wrapper around [ init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html) and

[, and is useful for simple applications that need a terminal with reasonable defaults for the entire lifetime of the application.](https://docs.rs/fn.restore.html)

`restore`See the [module-level documentation](https://docs.rs/init/index.html) for a comparison of all initialization
functions and guidance on when to use each one.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

A simple example where the app logic is contained in the closure:

```
use crossterm::event;
fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    ratatui::run(|terminal| {
        loop {
            terminal.draw(|frame| frame.render_widget("Hello, world!", frame.area()))?;
            if event::read()?.is_key_press() {
                break Ok(());
            }
        }
    })
}
```
A more complex example where the app logic is contained in a separate function:

```
use crossterm::event;
type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, Box<dyn std::error::Error>>;
fn main() -> Result<()> {
    ratatui::run(app)
}
fn app(terminal: &mut ratatui::DefaultTerminal) -> Result<()> {
    const GREETING: &str = "Hello, world!";
    loop {
        terminal.draw(|frame| frame.render_widget(format!("{GREETING}"), frame.area()))?;
        if matches!(event::read()?, event::Event::Key(_)) {
            break Ok(());
        }
    }
}
```
Once the app logic becomes more complex, it may be beneficial to move the app logic into a separate struct. This allows the app logic to be split into multiple methods with each having access to the state of the app. This can make the app logic easier to understand and maintain.

```
use crossterm::event;
type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, Box<dyn std::error::Error>>;
fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let mut app = App::new();
    ratatui::run(|terminal| app.run(terminal))
}
struct App {
    should_quit: bool,
    name: String,
}
impl App {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            should_quit: false,
            name: "world".to_string(),
        }
    }
    fn run(&mut self, terminal: &mut ratatui::DefaultTerminal) -> Result<()> {
        while !self.should_quit {
            terminal.draw(|frame| frame.render_widget("Hello, world!", frame.area()))?;
            self.handle_events()?;
        }
        Ok(())
    }
    fn render(&mut self, frame: &mut ratatui::Frame) -> Result<()> {
        let greeting = format!("Hello, {}!", self.name);
        frame.render_widget(greeting, frame.area());
        Ok(())
    }
    fn handle_events(&mut self) -> Result<()> {
        if event::read()?.is_key_press() {
            self.should_quit = true;
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

# init in ratatui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ratatui/0.30.2/ratatui/fn.init.html

`pub fn init() -> `[DefaultTerminal](https://docs.rs/type.DefaultTerminal.html)**crate feature**only.

`crossterm`## Expand description

Initialize a terminal with reasonable defaults for most applications.

This will create a new [ DefaultTerminal](https://docs.rs/type.DefaultTerminal.html) and initialize it with the following defaults:

- Backend: `CrosstermBackend``Stdout`
- Raw mode is enabled
- Alternate screen buffer enabled
- A panic hook is installed that restores the terminal before panicking. Ensure that this method is called after any other panic hooks that may be installed to ensure that the terminal is restored before those hooks are called.

For more control over the terminal initialization, use [ Terminal::new](https://docs.rs/struct.Terminal.html#method.new) or

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Terminal.html#method.with_options)

`Terminal::with_options`Ensure that this method is called *after* your app installs any other panic hooks to ensure the
terminal is restored before the other hooks are called.

Generally, use this function instead of [ try_init](https://docs.rs/fn.try_init.html) to ensure that the terminal is restored
correctly if any of the initialization steps fail. If you need to handle the error yourself, use

[instead.](https://docs.rs/fn.try_init.html)

`try_init`See the [module-level documentation](https://docs.rs/init/index.html) for a comparison of all initialization
functions and guidance on when to use each one.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This function will panic if any of the following steps fail:

- Enabling raw mode
- Entering the alternate screen buffer
- Creating the terminal fails due to being unable to calculate the terminal size

# restore in ratatui - Rust

`pub fn restore()`**crate feature**only.

`crossterm`## Expand description

Restores the terminal to its original state.

This function should be called before the program exits to ensure that the terminal is restored to its original state.

This function will attempt to restore the terminal to its original state by performing the following steps:

- Raw mode is disabled.
- The alternate screen buffer is left.

If either of these steps fail, the error is printed to stderr and ignored.

Use this function over [ try_restore](https://docs.rs/fn.try_restore.html) when you don’t need to handle the error yourself, as
ignoring the error is generally the correct behavior when cleaning up before exiting. If you
need to handle the error yourself, use

[instead.](https://docs.rs/fn.try_restore.html)
